that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to approve and confirm the convention between Canada and the United States of America for the preservation of the halibut fishery of the northern Pacific ocean and Bering sea, signed by Canada and the United States of America in Ottawa, on the 2nd of March, 1953, and to provide for the carrying 6ut of the provisions thereof.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
maintopic: FISHERIES
subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the house has already been informed of the purpose of the convention. That information was given in a statement made earlier at this session, on the day the convention was signed.
(Mr. Knowles.]
The purpose of this resolution is to secure parliamentary approval for a revised convention for the preservation of halibut in the northern Pacific ocean and the Bering sea. There are four changes in the new convention, the first of which is in respect of the actual name of the treaty.
When the treaty was first signed in 1923 it was known as the international fisheries treaty. It was the only international fisheries treaty at that time. Since then there has been a series of international treaties signed by Canada for the preservation of fisheries on our coasts and the costs of other countries. It has been thought that we must now be more specific in our designation of this commission, and the commission will henceforth be known as the international Pacific halibut commission.
The second change is made at the request of the Americans. In the United States the control of fisheries rests principally with the states rather than with the federal government. In the past, as their representatives, the Americans have had as their two commissioners one representative of the federal government and one of the state of Washington. The Americans would now like to give representation to the territory of Alaska, and have asked that the number of commissioners for each country be extended to three, so that they may make that provision.
The third change will give authority to the commission to establish more than one season for the catching of halibut. At the present time the scientists of the commission set the total catch to be made each year, and when that catch has been made the season is ended. Actually it now takes less than two months of fishing on the halibut banks off the Queen Charlotte islands to catch the quota which last year I think was 62 million pounds.
The scientists feel that instead of having just one open season it might be better to have two or perhaps even three at different times of the year in order to exploit fully the different banks. The industry is interested in this because it will mean that instead of having one catch which would have to be held in cold storage for ten months, the fish will remain in the sea and two or three open seasons will allow the fish to be caught at more regular intervals.
The last change is a very minor one. While fishing on the halibut banks themselves is controlled, halibut can be caught on the west coast in other areas incidental to fishing for cod or sole or other ground fish. We have had regulations to control the disposal of such halibut when caught

during the closed season, but there have been no regulations to control halibut caught incidental to other fishing during the open halibut season. The new convention makes provision for that.
When the bill is given second reading it is proposed to refer it to the standing committee on marine and fisheries.

maintopic: FISHERIES
subtopic: CONVENTION FOR PRESERVATION OF HALIBUT FISHERY OF NORTH PACIFIC OCEAN AND BERING SEA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are indebted to the minister for giving us a brief review of the changes being made in connection with the international fisheries commission which is now to be called the international Pacific halibut commission. The international fisheries commission has been giving general satisfaction during the time it has been in operation, which is some 30 years. There have been one or two minor changes made since the commission was started in 1923, but the major changes now being suggested are the result of considerable discussion which has taken place on the Pacific coast as to the advisability of introducing further revisions to the original treaty.
The reason for the change in the name is quite obvious. I understand that all the powers of the original commission are contained in the present convention.
I should like to examine briefly one of the major changes which are being made, namely, the splitting of the halibut season. As I said previously, discussions have been taking place which resulted in its being considered advisable to split the season. I think it has been the desire of the smaller fishing companies and the individual fishermen that such a change should be authorized. It would enable the owner of a small fishing vessel to catch halibut during the halibut season and then be able to catch other species of fish during the closed season for halibut. As the seasons for different species sometimes overlap, it is desirable to have this split season so that the fishermen may go out and for part of the time catch halibut and then perhaps catch salmon, and then later on in the year, during the second or third portions of the season, catch halibut again. That would seem to be advantageous, particularly to the smaller fishing concerns.
I understand that it has not been possible until now to authorize a split season because the scientists have been doubtful whether it would be in the best interests of conservation
Halibut Fishery Convention I should like to ask whether this split season will enable the quota of halibut to be increased. I understand at present it is in the neighbourhood of 55 or 56 million pounds each year. Possibly a decision has not yet been reached as to whether the quota can be increased, but my understanding is that the scientists believe that by splitting the season it will be possible, perhaps in the near future, to increase the quota without affecting the yield in future years. I hope the minister will be able to say something with regard to this.
The number of representatives on the commission has been increased and I understand that Canada is now to have three members, the same as the United States. 1 presume they will be appointed by this government and not by the province, in the same way that the members of the United States group are to be appointed, one from Alaska and one from the other states. Perhaps it will be possible for the minister to give the committee the names of the representatives. I notice that the treaty fixed the salaries to be paid and perhaps the minister could say a word on that.
My understanding is that the clause dealing with incidental catches merely extends the regulations, which are now applicable during the season when halibut cannot be caught, to the period when halibut can be caught.
I think these are all the points that I have to make in connection with this new convention. My understanding is that it is acceptable to the industry and to those officials who are responsible for the conservation of fish.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before I answer the points raised may 1 first of all express my appreciation of the manner in which the convention has been received. The proof of the pudding is in the eating, of course, and the thirty years of international halibut control have been a wonderful thing for the industry on the west coast. The hon. member for Nanaimo asked whether split seasons would result in a quota increase. The bill does not say that there are to be split seasons. The bill will make provision to give the commission authority, if the scientists so recommend, to have split seasons. What will probably happen will be that the next season will be split and the scientists will watch the results.
The scientists do feel that there are some banks on which halibut are not mature at the time of the open season on the main banks. If the fishing could be conducted later on these banks it would be possible to have a larger catch, but that will be a matter to be determined by scientific control. Certainly the quota will not be less because of the split season. He mentioned the fact that this convention has resulted in a very happy relationship both between ourselves and the Americans, and within the industry between fishermen, operators and the scientists of the international halibut commission.
The representatives for Canada are appointed by the federal government. At the moment we have just two and the Americans have just two under the existing convention. Our two representatives are the assistant deputy minister, Mr. George Clark, who is a product of the west coast and who was in the halibut fishery for many years, and a representative of the fishermen and industry, Mr. George Nickerson of Prince Rupert. When the commission is expanded to three we would hope to be able to have a representative of the fishermen and a representative of the processors instead of just a single representative for these groups. The commissioners get no payment. They get their expenses but no payment even on a per diem basis. That is also true of the other fisheries commissions.

That situation does not raise a problem as far as the government representative is concerned, nor does it raise too great a problem as far as the representative of the industry is concerned, but it does present a problem with respect to the fishermen's representative who has to take time off from his job of fishing in order to sit on these commissions. Both we and the Americans are now reviewing the position with respect to some sort of payment for attendance at the meetings.
A question was asked by the hon. member for Kamloops as to the effect on our relationships with the Russians in the north Pacific. This treaty actually has covered the waters of the north Pacific from San Diego up the American coast, up the British Columbia coast, up the Alaskan Panhandle and around into the United States half of the Bering sea. At the moment there is nothing to prohibit the Russians, or for that matter the people of any other maritime nation, from sending their ships into the deep sea offshore waters of that area to fish for halibut. The first real step forward in that regard is the new convention which was passed by the house a little earlier in this session, the Canadian-United States-Japanese treaty for the control of the fisheries in the north Pacific, under which each of these nations agrees to abstain from fishing offshore in the other nations' areas for those stocks which are under scientific study, which are under proper protection and control, and which are being fully exploited.
On our side of the Pacific that includes today the salmon, the halibut and the herring. So far as the Russians are concerned, at the moment they are not competitors at all in fishing in the north Pacific. It is the Japanese of course who are the great fishers on the east side of the Pacific. This convention is one of the treaties which will be respected under the new Canadian-United States-Japanese convention. We have the halibut under full scientific study, full conservation and control, and we are fully exploiting the fisheries.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. Sinclair thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 341, to implement a convention between Canada and the United States for the preservation of the halibut fishery.	.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

maintopic: FISHERIES

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of holding up second reading of the bill but I would be remiss in my duty if I were to allow second reading to pass without expressing to the government the great satisfaction which will be felt by the halibut fishermen of the Pacific coast that the treaty has been amended in the form that it has. It would be too much to expect any hon. member other than myself to remember that I spoke at some length on this subject on the 28th of June, 1950, at which time I urged upon the government revision of the treaty to make provision for split seasons, giving reasons therefor, and also giving the consensus of opinion of the fishermen of the Pacific coast. They will welcome this most heartily.
I should also like to say that the provision enabling the United States to appoint a commissioner representing Alaska is one which meets with the wholehearted approval and support of the fishermen of the Pacific coast. Canada, as the minister has said, will now appoint an additional commissioner. Without implying any criticism whatever of those already appointed, I would urge in the strongest manner possible that the third commissioner should be one with a practical knowledge and appreciation of the problems of halibut fishing from the point of view of the men who actually go out and catch the fish. I can assure the minister that the convention in its present form will have the wholehearted support of those who catch halibut on the Pacific coast.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, just before the house rose on Monday evening, while we were considering clause 4 of this bill, the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings was good enough to refer to my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and myself in very kindly words. The hon. member for Greenwood went a step further and included the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings himself in the kindly references. He further made the beneficent suggestion that if the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings and I would confer we might be able to clear up the little difficulty which seemed to be developing about clause 4. That advice was acted upon. As a result, I would like now to propose three amendments to clause 4 which I hope will commend themselves to all hon. members of the house.
One of the points discussed when we were considering clause 4 was the provision for an extension of the period within which those persons who were members of the forces as of June 21, 1952, might elect as their place of residence for purposes of having their votes recorded. As the house will remember, that period expired on September 21, 1952. We have since found that approximately
20,000	personnel had not at that date made their election. The amendment proposed in clause 4 is to the effect that these "delinquents" should have until dissolution of parliament to make their election. There was some suggestion the other evening that there ought to be a fixed time limit as an alternative to the date of dissolution. The amendment which I will ask one of my colleagues to move will provide that persons in the class I have mentioned will have two months from the date that this amending bill is assented to to make their election or until dissolution, whichever shall occur first.
In considering the voting regulations governing members of the forces, paragraph 27, of the Canadian forces voting regulations, which the house will remember is a schedule to the elections act, provides that as soon as possible after the publication of the notice in daily orders on form 5 setting out that the house has been dissolved, the date of the election and other details which I do not think I need to give the house, the commanding officer shall prepare a list of names. There was some feeling among members that the words "as soon as possible"
4210	HOUSE OF
Canadian Forces Act
with which the clause begins were perhaps too indefinite and it was therefore suggested that there be a definite time specified rather than a nebulous period. X will therefore ask that paragraph 27 be amended by deleting "as soon as possible" and substituting for those words the words "within two weeks".
The third amendment is a consequential one which provides for renumbering of the subclauses of clause 4. If the house permits I would like to have my colleague move three amendments to clause 4 to give effect to what I have briefly stated.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

Mr. Fournier (Hull) moves:
That clause 4 be amended by deleting lines 7, 8 and 9 and substituting therefor the following:
"(2) Before the dissolution of the twenty-first parliament or before the expiration of two months from the day on which the Canadian Forces Act, 1953, was assented to, whichever is the earlier, every member of the regular forces who was such a member on the twenty-first day of June, 1952, shall" and also

" and also

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that the kindly words which I directed the other night towards the Associate Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration were justified by the results which have accrued. I am not sure whether the suggestion of the hon. member for Greenwood added to that situation, but at least the three working together yesterday I think accomplished in this matter something which is a distinct improvement over what we had in the committee the night before last.
I still think that it was unfortunate that the situation had to arise regarding these


amendments. I think they are an improvement upon that which was originally brought in but the situation is still not as good as it would have been if the report of the elections committee last year had been acted upon and the necessary steps taken at that time. However, as that was not done, we were faced with an unfortunate situation. I know that yesterday both ministers tried to meet the views which were expressed and in the end the amendments which are brought before the committee this morning, although not the most satisfactory in the world, are a definite improvement, and I am sure since it was necessary to have them they will contribute towards the working of the regulations.
I might say that in our discussions yesterday we all thought of other amendments which perhaps could have been made and which would have improved the regulations. I am sure that in some future time after we have had the experience of trying these amendments they will be subject to review. When that does take place, whatever committee is operating at that time should try to re-establish the principle which was established last year.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS

Shall the amendments
carry?

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not quite clear on the purport of the second amendment as far as the lists are concerned. As I understand the matter, the commanding officer of each unit will have a list prepared and I think the amendment provides that it will be sent to the deputy returning officer. Does that mean that the list which is prepared by the commanding officer might very readily contain the names of men who are going to vote in a hundred or more different constituencies? Does it mean that the names of men who are going to vote in each particular constituency are to be sent to the deputy returning officer of that constituency-or is there just this one list which contains the names of people voting in a large number of constituencies and which will be in the unit office and available for inspection?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am not
familiar with the exact routine that is followed. It must be in accordance with what is set out in the regulations and paragraph 27 thereof provides that each commanding officer after publication of this order shall, through the liaison officer, furnish to the special returning officer for the appropriate voting territory a list of names of Canadian forces electors attached to his unit with ranks, numbers and places of ordinary residence, as described in paragraph 23 which we are amending. Whatever

detailed procedure the commanding officer follows in that regard is not being changed in any event. The only change is that instead of an indefinite time, which might be interpreted differently by different people, his duty as indicated here is limited to a period of two weeks. In other words, he must have the list of his unit prepared and forwarded to the special returning officer, not in an indefinite period but within two weeks. Otherwise, the procedure followed is whatever the routine is in regard to this section.
I am not familiar with the step by step details of the duties of the commanding officer.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I take it that this list
prepared by each C.O. will be available in his own office where it can be inspected by the local candidate. In addition to that, I presume he sends a copy of this list to the special returning officer who will be, I suppose, an officer at national defence headquarters. I presume that officer will then make a consolidated list of these people, and will have a list of the men voting in each particular constituency, which list will be available in Ottawa. I should like to ask the minister if these lists will be available to the candidates.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not going to presume anything in regard to the procedure, but as I understand it the lists that are prepared pursuant to the sections are available for inspection by any person concerned. It is for that purpose they are made. Just how that is done or what steps are taken to accomplish it I cannot say. I am not familiar with it.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think we should have
something a little more definite than that. The minister says he is not familiar with this matter, but none of us is familiar with it. Just reading the regulations the only conclusion to which one can come is that there will be a list for each unit in the particular unit office and there will also be a copy of the list sent to this special returning officer who will be here at national defence headquarters. I think the minister should be able to tell us whether this consolidated list at national defence headquarters will be available, because it would be the only list from which candidates from any particular constituency could find out what people are going to vote in their constituency.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I shall get that information in a moment.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Dealing with subsection 2
which is mandatory in that it says that every member of the forces shall, after the
Canadian Forces Act
expiration of a time or within two months after the date when this act has been given royal assent, do certain things, I should like to point out that the average soldier, sailor or airman would never know when this act was given the royal assent. What opportunity has a man serving in Korea or on a ship, or even in a station in Canada, to know when this act has been given the royal assent? It seems to me quite unreasonable to expect a private soldier or able seaman, who is not particularly interested in politics, to know when the act has received the royal assent.
Surely, the obligation of informing the individual man through the normal channels should rest on the minister. He should inform the men when the royal assent has been given, and then they could be required to sign the necessary forms. It seems to me that if that is not done, then a very unfair obligation is placed on the serving man.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: As I intimated on Monday evening when this section was under consideration, it is proposed that when the terminating date is established by royal assent to this bill the position will be fully set out in orders. We are contemplating also-we have not firmly decided this as yet-writing to each one of the men who have not elected, setting out what is open to him and the time within which it must be done. We are anxious, as I am sure all hon. members of the house are anxious, that every possible step be taken to decrease to the lowest possible number those people who have not elected and who may therefore have to be dealt with at the poll on polling day. At the moment we are studying all possible means which might be effective to that end. I can assure the hon. member that the matter will be given every attention by the department, by the minister and also by the services who are anxious to have the matter cleared up as completely as possible.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I think it is more than a matter of writing letters. The discussion which took place about these amendments was based on the fact that the department requires more time to get these declarations. The average person felt that the period of two months was too long, and it should be shorter. We realize, however, that there are troops scattered throughout Korea and western Europe. The department felt it needed time in which to ensure that as many of these men as possible had signed. The department can write letters if they want to do so, but I doubt if that is the best way of dealing with this. If, when the minister leaves this building today, he were to cause

Canadian Forces Act
a signal to go out to every commanding officer of every unit in the world, I have enough confidence in the efficiency of these officers and men to believe that they would see to it that within two weeks 90 per cent of the men would be pledged. I think that is the procedure which should be adopted; at least, that is why we think too much time is being taken.
In so far as the lists are concerned, to which the hon. member for Calgary East refers, this is the first time that provision has appeared permitting access to these lists. It was not there before. I might say for the benefit of the minister, who has not had experience with the administration of the lists and some of his officials who have not had that experience, that in many cases these lists were not prepared at all. I think, if the minister is going to write any letters, they should be letters to the commanding officer giving directions as to how this matter should be carried out, and impressing upon him the fact that the best qualified officers and N.C.O.'s should be detailed to do the work.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The minister has not
answered my question.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Dealing with that question, it is now my understanding that the commanding officer prepares a list of the personnel of his unit, together with their place of residence, and in addition to sending it to the special returning officer for the respective territory, of which there are three in Canada, also sends a copy-perhaps I should read that provision:
-the commanding officer shall also furnish to the deputy returning officer a copy of such list for the taking of the votes of the Canadian forces electors attached to his unit; at any reasonable time during an election, such list and the statements referred to in paragraph 23 shall be open to inspection by any officially nominated candidate or his accredited representative, and such persons shall be permitted to make extracts therefrom.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The difficulty I see is how
a candidate or his accredited representative could see this list. How does he know where it is going to be? A member for a Nova Scotia constituency may quite readily have a couple of hundred people stationed in Calgary, Alberta. How is the candidate or his representative to see the list? Naturally, he is not going to be able to see it in Calgary. As I understand what the minister has said, these lists are sent to three particular places in Canada for the forces as a whole, and in each case the list is sent to the special returning officer for this area. Now, is it at the area that the candidate or his representative will see these lists, or where is it?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: He may see lists either at the unit through the deputy returning officer or through the special returning officer of the area. In either place all these names are available.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Let us take a practical example. Let us take a constituency in Nova Scotia. In Calgary there are a couple of hundred people from that constituency who will be registered in that constituency in Nova Scotia. Where are the candidates in that constituency in Nova Scotia going to see these lists? They cannot travel out to Calgary; they have not facilities for appointing agents in Calgary, and so forth.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: As I understand the regulations, if the candidate or the accredited representative of a candidate wants to check across the country he must do so through representatives in the different places. I do not think there are any provisions otherwise in the regulations as they exist now and as they were put in the statute by the committee which considered this matter.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps we can find out what an area consists of. Is there any sort of master list made for all the units for the particular area concerned which the candidates or the candidates' representatives could look at and get the people from their own constituency?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
To answer the first question, according to the regulations special returning officers are appointed (a) for Ontario and Quebec; (b) for the maritimes; (c) for the western provinces and lastly in areas where Canadian forces are serving overseas, such areas being as designated by the chief electoral officer.
I am informed that so far as these lists are concerned they are not, as the hon. member calls it, master lists; they are lists as they cpme in from the emits to the special returning officer in the area.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Do these lists also come into any central office here at national headquarters where they might be available?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No, I am informed they do not. Once the election is called, the administration of these regulations, as I understand it-except in these particulars where commanding officers are specifically authorized or instructed to do some duty-is under the jurisdiction of the chief electoral officer the same as all other administrative regulations in regard to voting. He is the man who interprets and carries out these regulations. The taking of the vote is not a matter of administration for the army as such nor for the Department of National Defence.

These regulations set out the duties that the officers and personnel of the Department of National Defence have to perform but the actual carrying out of the electoral regulations is not within our jurisdiction. It is under the jurisdiction rather of the chief electoral officer.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is not the matter of carrying out the vote that I am talking about.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: In regard to lists or anything else pertaining to the election, all is under the chief electoral officer who, I take it, is governed by the regulations.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The point is that the act
provides that the candidate or his representatives shall have access to these lists and see the lists; but from the practical point of view, if the lists are posted up in the hundreds of different stations across Canada, or are available in hundreds of different stations where troops are to be found across Canada, that provision really means absolutely nothing. Unless there is, or are, some central place or places where these lists are available, the provision might just as well not be there. That is what I am getting at, as to whether these lists can be made available at some central area. It seems to me there should not be any undue difficulty in having that done. Is the minister going to comment on that? What is to prevent these lists being sent here to national defence headquarters and being available here?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not think I can make
any comment beyond this. I will certainly see that the observations of the hon. member are taken into consideration. I do not think I can say anything more.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Will the candidate or his
agent be able to see not only the lists of personnel who would record votes in his constituency, but the places where all the other service personnel in that station will be recording their votes?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I understand the list shows
the places of residence of all the members of the units, together with the places where they are resident for the purpose of casting their vote.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Shall the section as
amended carry?

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
May I ask one question on
subsection 2. There is an addition there. The addition reads:
But where the member is serving outside Canada or in a ship and none of the foregoing clauses (a), '!*'. or (c) is applicable-
Canadian Forces Act
It seems to me that there may be certain personnel in these services to whom these clauses will not be applicable, and who will not have had any place of ordinary residence in Canada at the time of enlistment. For instance, suppose a person enlisted into the armed forces from outside Canada. We have certain musicians from Holland who were enlisting in the armed forces of Canada. I do not know that they would have a vote, but there would certainly be men from the United Kingdom who will have joined the armed forces in the United Kingdom, and perhaps are now serving in western Europe. The time will come, if it has not already been reached, when they will be eligible to vote in Canada. They would never have had any ordinary place of residence in Canada, and none of the three clauses (a) (b) or (c>
would be applicable.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In reply to the hon. member, I understand that this particular portion of the clause which he is reading was designed to cover the cases he has mentioned. If a man has the right to vote, he must have come into Canada once and gone out to make the clause applicable, in which event his place of residence would be where he was while in Canada. If a man has never been in Canada I do not think he is covered.
It would appear to me that if he had a spouse or relative in Canada, under the right of election section he could take the residence of his spouse or other dependent or relative. If he has no relative in Canada and has never been in Canada even for a day, I doubt whether he would have the right to vote under the regulations.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would he not have the right to vote if he had served the required time in the Canadian armed forces? Would that not entitle him to citizenship?

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext: I understand not unless he had actually been in Canada; but if he has served for that length of time in practically all cases he would have been in Canada at some time at least for a day. There might be one type of person who would not fit into any of these particular regulations. I do not think they would be very numerous.

maintopic: CANADIAN FORCES ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO NATIONAL DEFENCE ACT, DEFENCE SERVICES PENSION ACT AND CANADIAN FORCES VOTING REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes; I think you might have men who enlisted in the United Kingdom, perhaps men who had been in Canada with the R.A.F. and had received their training here, but then they would not have been members of the Canadian forces. There must be a certain number of men who are
4214	HOUSE OF
Canadian Forces Act
enlisted directly from European countries or from the United Kingdom who will be serving in the armed forces of Canada and who, it may be assumed, will take their leave, and all that sort of thing, in the United Kingdom. They would have no permanent residence here. These persons do not seem to be provided for, when they become entitled to a vote.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need add much to what was said last night in the discussion on the resolution preceding the bill. The proposed amendment to the Canadian Broadcasting Act, 1936, provides authority for granting to the corporation out of the consolidated revenue fund amounts that equal the taxes collected under the Excise Tax Act on the sale of sound broadcasting sets and apparatus, and similarly for granting to the corporation, on account of television, an amount equal to the taxes collected under the Excise Tax Act on the sale of television receiving sets and tubes.
The proposed amendment continues the provision of funds to the corporation by statutory provision, and does not alter the basic principle for the provision of adequate funds to the corporation, therefore retaining the autonomy which is inherent in the present legislation.
The proposed amendment is one section in the bill, and the repetition of that section also appears. The second one will be repealed when the Revised Statutes of Canada come into effect.
Hon. members will recall that already at this session we have considered Bill No. 225, to amend the Excise Tax Act, and that it has been passed. Section 11 in that bill made provision for the repeal of section 6 in schedule I, and section 6 (a) was substituted therefor. I need not read it in full, but that section now refers to phonographs,

record playing devices, radio broadcasting receiving sets or any combination of the foregoing, and the tubes therefor; and states that they shall be subject to a tax of 15 per cent. Then paragraph (b) deals with television apparatus, and makes specific reference to television receiving sets and tubes therefor, as well as any apparatus or device that enables a person to see, or to see and hear, television programs distributed by any means whatever, or television radio broadcasting programs distributed by any means whatever. And in that case, again, the tax is 15 per cent.
If hon. members will recall the discussion that took place when that bill was before the house they will recall that it had, as its purpose, the clarification of all those things included that would have to do with television sets, and this included what are known as rediffusion sets.
I believe that is all the comment I have to make at this time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was some discussion last night at the resolution stage, and I do not propose to repeat now what I said at that time. I do draw attention to the fact, however, that the bill is open to all the objections to which, in my remarks last night, I said it was open, having regard to the observations of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) at the resolution stage and those of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) when he referred to this matter in his budget speech.
The amendment to the act is very brief. It may be simple in appearance; nevertheless it has the effect of setting up continuing legislation under which revenue will be paid over out of the consolidated revenue fund by the Minister of Finance year by year to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, without any further reference to parliament and without need of any further authority from parliament. That is a fundamentally unsound procedure, having regard to the necessity of maintaining strict parliamentary control over all moneys drawn from the consolidated revenue fund.
The minister has said this amendment continues in effect the scheme that has been in existence for a long time. It is quite true that under the combined effect of the Radio Act and the Broadcasting Act as in effect hitherto, the $2.50 licence fee on radio receiving sets has been paid over, under statutory authority, by the government to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. But hon. members will recall that parliament was
Canadian Broadcasting Act called upon each year to make provision in a specific item of the estimates for the collection of that radio receiving licence fee. Parliament was thus afforded an opportunity every year at least to debate this whole question.
Under the amendment before us there is no such right. There will not be anything before parliament-unless, by any chance, in his budget proposals the Minister of Finance recommends some change in the excise tax, either by way of the percentage of the tax or in the matter of its application.
I think the house ought to understand clearly that if the amendment is passed in its present form, this will be an end to any annual opportunity for discussion as to whether parliament should make provision in this form and in these amounts for the needs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I indicated last night that there may be a specious coincidence in amounts as between the amount collected hitherto from licence fees on radio receiving sets and the amount it is calculated will be paid under this new amendment to the corporation for sound broadcasting, being the amount collected by way of excise tax on radio receiving sets and tubes. That happens to be a coincidence and it is nothing more. It is no excuse for ignoring and defying sound parliamentary principles.
It was indicated last night that if given second reading this bill will be referred to the committee on radio broadcasting where it will be further reviewed. If that course is followed I hope the committee will be prepared to propose amendments to this bill because in its present form it is open to the serious charge that it simply lifts control over a substantial amount of money year by year completely out of the hands of parliament. If this measure is passed in this form the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) can go on from now until eternity paying out of the consolidated revenue fund all the amounts collected from the excise tax on the goods mentioned in section 6 of schedule I of the Excise Tax Act. I consider that that is an utterly unsound way of proceeding.
As I said to the house last night, there are additional reasons why parliament should consider this matter annually, why parliament should address itself in each annual session to the consideration of how much it ought to provide to meet the proper expenses of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, both with respect to sound broadcasting and to television. These are matters of vast importance. Because it happens at this particular moment that the amount that the

Trade with China and North Korea
government thinks will be required for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation happens to coincide approximately with the amount that is being yielded at this time from the excise tax on the goods in section 6 of schedule I of the Excise Tax Act, we are being asked to pass this legislation giving the minister power to pay over all the amounts collected from this Excise Tax Act to the corporation.
That is no way to go about meeting this problem. This coincidence in amounts that exists today may not exist in six months' or a year's time. I do not think one would be rash to say that it will not exist in two years' time, in three years' time or in four years' time. Then why do we pass legislation of this kind which has the effect that from now until eternity parliament will not have an annual opportunity of reviewing this whole matter?
This is not doing justice to the obligations of parliament with reference to the very important task that it has placed upon the shoulders of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Surely they are entitled to have their affairs and financial needs carefully considered year by year in parliament. If this bill is passed in its present form it will preclude that. I say that if the bill is given second reading I hope the committee on radio broadcasting will be able to send back a much better bill than the one that is now before us.

maintopic: EMERGENCY POWERS ACT-ORDER IN COUNCIL RE TRADE WITH MAINLAND CHINA AND NORTH KOREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks that I should like to make with reference to the amendment introduced last evening by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), to the motion that the house resolve itself into committee of supply. This matter is of recent origin, going back to what happened in the house just two days ago.


May I recall to hon. members precisely what happened in this house on Monday morning of this week, this being Wednesday morning. Among other items of business the house had before it for consideration a number of amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. This bill had been before the house previously, but the house in committee of the whole reviewed the various amendments on Monday morning. It was noted at the time that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) did not remain in the house to pilot the amendments through the committee of the whole, but left the chamber. The amendments were approved in due course, the bill was given third reading and passed on its way to the other place.
After the house had spent but a few minutes . in the transaction of some other business, to the surprise of hon. members the Minister of Transport made his appearance just prior to the one o'clock adjournment and proceeded to ask permission to revert to motions. That permission was granted and he thereupon tabled two copies, in English and in French, of order in council P.C. 1953604, passed on Friday, April 17, under the provisions of the Emergency Powers Act with respect to the control of trade by sea with mainland China and North Korea.
The full significance of what the government has done I think is now abundantly apparent. This was an order in council made in the usual secrecy last Friday. The government must have known about this matter for weeks in advance. In any event they made this order on Friday, April 17. They had ample opportunity last Friday night in announcing the business that would come before the house on Monday, April 20, to refer to this matter. That would have been the time, if they were determined to proceed by order in council, to have acquainted the house with the fact. Much better still, that was the time to notify the house that amendments would be proposed on Monday morning, when the Canada Shipping Act amendments were before the house, to carry into legislative effect in the proper constitutional and parliamentary manner what the government has now done by this order in council.
But, no, the government did not proceed in that manner. The government did not choose to acquaint the house with the facts on Friday evening. The government did not choose to acquaint the house with the fact on motions on Monday morning. Why was it that the government did not take advantage of the opportunity to have announced this order in council on motions? Oh, no, this order was held back, and held back deliberately, until

the house had concluded its consideration of the amendments to the Canada Shipping Act. Nothing could be more obvious.
They did not want this subject discussed in parliament. That is equally obvious. Therefore they held it back until the Canada Shipping Act amendments were out of the way. Is this the kind of method that hon. members of this house are going to approve? I put that question to hon. members of this house who are accustomed to support this government. I ask every one of them if he approves the way in which the government has flouted and ignored this House of Commons and denied to the House of Commons information on a matter of very considerable importance as to which there would have been an opportunity on Monday morning for adequate discussion in the parliamentary manner. That is question No. 1, Mr. Speaker.
Let us follow that a little further. How did the government proceed? Where did they seek to find a method of dealing with the problem, a problem that was described by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) last night in his very angry and ill-tempered speech as contraband trade? This House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, does not take second place to the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the government in its determination to see that proper measures are taken to prevent trade in contraband with. communist China. Why does the government not trust the House of Commons? The House of Commons is capable of prompt action. It has shown that on more than one occasion where conditions required prompt action. But oh no, the government did not choose the parliamentary method. They wanted to do this by their secret and favourite method of legislating by order in council.
They might have approached the matter through the Canada Shipping Act, but they did not do so. They went to a statute which has now acquired a very ugly and notorious history, the Emergency Powers Act. This is a measure that has had as much discussion at the present session as any measure that has come before the house. No legislative measure that has come before the house this year has been subjected to as lengthy debate or as critical comment as the bill to extend the Emergency Powers Act.
That measure was criticized because of the breadth of the powers that the government sought to take from parliament to do virtually everything that parliament can do with the exception of taxation, arrest, detention and deportation. Everything else in the way of transfer of absolute powers they grasped from parliament. When we in this quarter of the
22, 1953
Trade with China and North Korea house criticized that measure, when we said that no self-respecting parliament could pass a measure virtually abdicating its powers to the executive branch of government, we were told by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in the most soothing terms, in the intervention he made in the debate in its late stages on March 26, that the house need have no fear, that the government would be so careful in the exercise of these powers, that the utmost regard would be had for all democratic privileges and considerations, and that the house might well subdue all fears that it entertained about placing in the hands of the governor in council powers that could be used virtually to subvert the entire constitution of the country and stop all pretence of parliamentary government. Such was the assurance that the house received from the Prime Minister.
Some of us were very critical of the way in which the government in the two years that this measure has been in existence had proceeded to legislate by this method while parliament was in session and quite capable of providing anything required in the way of legislation. What was the record that we pointed out then? In 1951 nineteen orders in council were passed under the Emergency Powers Act and every one of them was passed while parliament was in session, because that year parliament sat from January 30 to December 29; and as to parliament being actually sitting while the orders were passed, every one of them was passed at a time when parliament was actually sitting and not in recess. In the year 1952 five orders in council were passed under the Emergency Powers Act, and three of the five were passed while parliament was actually sitting and quite capable of enacting anything that was required to meet any legislative lack at the time.
We raised this question and raised it repeatedly, and one would have thought that the government would have enough regard for the institution of parliament to have refrained from proceeding to legislate by this order in council method while parliament was actually in session. The order in council in question in this debate was passed on April 17, last Friday. The house was in session that day from eleven o'clock in the morning until ten o'clock at night. Again on Monday, April 20, the house was in session from eleven o'clock on, and I have already pointed out that a bill was under debate in the house that morning under which this measure could have been introduced by the government as a proper amendment to the Canada Shipping Act.
So, Mr. Speaker, we have it crystal clear that this government does not care whether

Trade with China and North Korea or not parliament is sitting. They have the powers under the Emergency Powers Act, and use those powers they will in whatever way they choose, whether parliament is sitting or not. In the view of the government, when a situation like this arises parliament as an institution might just as well not be in session. We might just as well pack our bags and go home so far as the government is concerned.

speechtext:
They do not take us into their confidence. They do not discuss problems of this kind with us. They just go ahead and follow their secret and favourite method of proceeding to legislate by order in council.
Let there be no doubt in the mind of any hon. member, Mr. Speaker, or in the mind of any Canadian that this is legislation. This is not some matter of regulation, some small matter that does not require the direct attention of parliament. This is not the sort of thing that parliament sometimes makes provision for by way of regulations to carry out the intent of a statute. This is legislation. No legislation enacted by parliament this year is more directly legislative in form or effect than order in council P.C. 1953-604.
We have here now-and let the public fully realize it-two law-making bodies. We have parliament containing the elected representatives of the people sitting here transacting public business in public for all to see and so that the public may form its judgment upon the way in which its business is done in parliament. At the same time we have another legislative body that meets in secret and by star chamber methods proceeds to pass legislation just as binding upon every Canadian as the legislation enacted here in parliament in due parliamentary form. Which is the democratic method? The parliamentary method is a method that has been tested down through the centuries and has been found to be the one method that will guarantee the preservation of the rights and liberties of the people. Long ago secret methods were found to be the kind that make it easy for executive bodies to trespass upon the rights of the people.
The executive branch of government, historically and in fact, has never been the champion of the rights of the people. It has been parliament and parliament alone that has fought the battles for the preservation of the rights and freedoms of the people. Parliament and the people have an opportunity now of seeing under their very eyes parliament proceeding to legislate in the traditional parliamentary and democratic method, and side by side a cabal consisting of twenty men proceeding to legislate by star
rMr. Fleming.]

chamber methods that were found three centuries ago to be so notorious that men were prepared to shed their blood to exterminate them. There was no occasion whatever, Mr. Speaker, no need whatever, for the governor in council to proceed by this method. Parliament was in session. Parliament was dealing with matters directly cognate with this very subject matter, and it would have been a relatively easy matter to have introduced this subject in the house on Monday morning by way of an amendment to the bill then under consideration in the house. So, Mr. Speaker, you will never have a more flagrant case than this of the government deliberately choosing to ignore parliament, abandoning parliamentary methods and proceeding to legislate in secret by order in council.
Now, sir, what were the excuses, the pretexts offered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) last night for this attack on parliament in his angry speech? There were two excuses which he gave, Mr. Speaker, and the first was that the end justifies the means.

maintopic: EMERGENCY POWERS ACT-ORDER IN COUNCIL RE TRADE WITH MAINLAND CHINA AND NORTH KOREA
speechtext: That is pretty flimsy.

maintopic: EMERGENCY POWERS ACT-ORDER IN COUNCIL RE TRADE WITH MAINLAND CHINA AND NORTH KOREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when parliament's position is at stake, when the parliamentary and democratic process is challenged, we of the official opposition say most directly to this government and to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the end cannot justify the means, when you deliberately choose autocratic and unparliamentary means. There is no excuse here for the way in which this government went about it. It was an empty and hollow pretext which the minister sought to put forward last night, and it will convince no one. I do not think that the minister even convinced himself.
Then the minister said: That is the way they did it in the United States and in the United Kingdom. Well, the minister ought to know perhaps better than most members of this house that under the system prevailing in the United States, with congress enacting general legislation, it is their policy and practice to leave matters to the executive branch of government which we, under our system of responsible government, would not think of vesting in the executive branch of the government-at least until this house came to be dominated by an autocratic administration here which had lost all knowledge of true parliamentary processes.
The reference on the part of the minister to the United Kingdom was indeed interesting because it sheds a clear light on something which the Minister of Trade and Commerce said last night in attempting to stampede this house into thinking that this was a

matter of real, desperate urgency. He said it was a time for action and not for talk. Well, you see that to his autocratic mentality parliament is just a place for talk, and therefore, he has no patience with it. He has shown that many and many a time. His mentality is obviously not adjusted to parliamentary processes because it is quite true that parliament is a place where people talk. That is the democratic method that has been found by a process of long experimentation to be the kind that is safe and the kind that preserves the rights and freedom of people-so that anything that even resembles talk is anathema to him. To the Minister of Trade and Commerce action is the thing that matters; action is what he demands. Well, the House of Commons is quite prepared to move as quickly as is required, Mr. Speaker.
As I have indicated, his references to the United Kingdom approach to this question have some very interesting light to shed upon the atmosphere of urgency that the Minister of Trade and Commerce sought to throw about this matter. What do we find, Mr. Speaker, to be the fact-the fact that was not stated to this house last night by the Minister of Trade and Commerce? When we look up the records of the United Kingdom we find that their order was made on March 13, 1953-over a month before this matter became one of such desperate urgency last Friday that this government could not even tolerate the idea of putting it before parliament. It was laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom on March 16, 1953, one month and one day before the cabinet here proceeded to pass this order in council. It came into operation on March 17, 1953, one month exactly before this government considered it necessary to pass this order in council-this notorious order in council.

When the house rose for the luncheon recess we were discussing the amendment that was proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) in respect to the order in council which was passed the other day while parliament was in session.
Last night I listened with a good deal of interest to the speeches that were made on that amendment. It is not necessary to repeat what the leader of this party said last evening in putting our position plainly before parliament in respect to this action and in respect to this amendment. Our leader said that we supported the amendment because we believed that it was a negation of the right of a democratic parliament. I do not believe there is one argument against that position. I believe the position taken by the government is indefensible.
Much was said last night with regard to the right thing being done the wrong way. Perhaps a good deal of emphasis was placed on that phrase. It is all very well for a government that does something in the wrong way to rise and point the finger at opposition members and say: "Well, did we do right?" Of course that is tantamount to putting the opposition on the spot, so that they will declare whether they agree with it or not. I do not believe it is a matter of doing the right thing in the wrong way at all. I think 68108-267
22, 1953	4221
Trade with China and North Korea it goes farther than that. It is a matter ot the government assuming that they are right, and that they alone are capable of determining what is right.
It is not so long ago, as a matter of fact, just a few short weeks ago, that we were discussing the Emergency Powers Act under which the government was able to pass this order in council. What arguments took place then? The whole opposition in that debate were opposed to that measure, mainly because the government assumed power under it to take action while parliament was in session. At the time the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) became more or less an apologist for the government along that line.
It amazes me, Mr. Speaker, that after that act was passed, after all the arguments were used, even after the Minister of Justice, by inference anyway, agreed that it was not the proper principle to apply, orders in council should without necessity be passed while parliament was in session. They wanted the powers of the Emergency Powers Act so that they would be able to do things in an emergency when parliament was not in session. It amazes me that just so soon after the passing of that act and the arguments put forth, the government has turned around and done the very thing which they admitted at the time was, under our democratic processes, an objectionable thing to do. How they could do that, I do not know. Even the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself, during the debate on the Emergency Powers Act, admitted that to pass orders in council while parliament was sitting was an objectionable thing to do.
I recall particularly the statements he made, although at the time he was talking particularly of a secret order which was passed in compliance with certain actions that were taken by the North Atlantic treaty nations. What did the Prime Minister say at that time? He said, as reported at page 3318 of Hansard:
All those who are parties to the North Atlantic alliance share with each other top secret Information because of our confidence that there are measures being taken for the proper protection against or the anticipation of sabotage and espionage.
It is unfortunate to have to live in a world where that has to be done. It is unfortunate that we cannot feel that everybody in the world is going to behave in a manner befitting a Christian gentleman, but that is not the world we are living in. There are certain things that we are reluctantly forced to do if we attempt to discharge the responsibilities that happen to be ours.
Well, as I say, I know he was talking about a particular secret order, and I am not one, and never have been one, to object

I have never criticized the government on the action they took at the time the spy scandal broke out in this country. I have never criticized them for setting up the commission to investigate that matter and denying counsel for the time being to those who were suspected of sabotage. I have never criticized them for that action. It was an emergency at the time. I do not think parliament was in session. It may have been, because I happened to live next door to Mr. Gouzenko's apartment, and I wondered what it was all about at the time. Unfortunately, that was the situation. The government took the bull by the horns and acted according to the power granted them. I have never criticized them for doing that. In fact, I believe I have said in my public meetings that it was the proper thing to do, that I would have done the same thing under ordinary circumstances. And I say "I"-but of course I never will have a responsibility of that kind.
I never have criticized the government for that. I do not criticize them for doing the right thing at the right time. But if, as the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself admitted in the debate on the Emergency Powers Act, to do such things would be objectionable, even though he were applying the law to a secret order, how much more objectionable is it when it is not necessary that the order be kept secret, and when parliament is sitting. Upon the face of it, and in the light of the government's own admission as stated by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the Prime Minister, how much more objectionable is this.
I say we have reasons for supporting the amendment of the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) in connection with the order in council which, as he says, was passed while parliament is sitting. I must admit that I do not know what happens in a cabinet meeting. I do not know how they discuss their orders in council.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am not ashamed of a single, solitary thing I have ever done in the political field or in this House of Commons.
Now, let me get back to the keyhole again, if I may. Here is an order in council, such as we are now discussing. The Prime Minister says, "Well, boys, we have this matter of ships entering Chinese ports"-and so forth and so on; or it may be something else. "What are we going to do about it?" Someone rises and says, "Well, it is the right thing to do." The Prime Minister says, "It may be the right thing, but do you not think that the way we should do it is not the right way?" The Minister of Trade and Commerce says, "Huh! Huh!"
I can imagine looking through that keyhole during a session of cabinet and the Minister of Trade and Commerce saying, "Huh". But when he has the nerve to say it in the House of Commons, that is too much for me. I cannot understand it.
Then the Prime Minister says, "Well perhaps we had better pass it." And the gentleman sitting at the end of the table, the Secretary of State (Mr. Bradley), is asked by the Prime Minister, "What do you think about it?"

The order in council is passed. Eventually it is laid on the table. And we are now in the process of debating whether or not it is a negation of the democratic rights of parliament. I say, and I do believe, that the government should admit it has made a mistake in doing what it has done while parliament is in session. It should tell us whether it was an order in council signed along with a million others, or whether it knew what it was doing at the time. Did they know what they were doing, right on the heels of their being given power by parliament under the Emergency Powers Act, and having been made aware of all the objections to exercising it while parliament was in session? When the Emergency Powers Act was passed we were given a number of explanations as to why the government felt that that act was necessary. As I recall it, one of them was the emergency of an apprehended election. We have heard no other justification; we have heard no satisfactory explanation as to why it was necessary to introduce and pass that Emergency Powers Act. The explanation of that act is that the government insisted it should be done.
It has now been drawn to my attention that there is not a cabinet minister in the house at the moment. I do not know whether I should make any other comment on that, other than saying that probably the reason is they are having a cabinet meeting to decide whether or not they should revoke this order in council. I hope that is what they are doing. But in the absence of any satisfactory explanation as to why the Emergency Powers Act was pushed through this house, we are left with the statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that it was because of the emergency of an apprehended election.
In the light of that statement, Mr. Speaker, we are faced with this situation from which I suggest there is only one obvious conclusion to draw. The government know that it had no basis in fact, no justification in fact, for having insisted on pushing the Emergency Powers Act through the house, and when they contemplated the necessity of justifying that action in the election campaign, in the emergency of an apprehended election, said


to themselves: "Well, we had better pass an order in council under the Emergency Powers Act to justify its existence and to justify our having passed it." And so they looked around and they decided: Well, we will dig up a subject which it will be difficult for parliament or anybody in the country to criticize us for having dealt with. And perhaps the best subject for us to pass an order in council on from that point of view is one that will prohibit the shipping of contraband to communist China. That was a ready-made and obvious subject for them to deal with, and so they decided to deal with it by order in council, and bring it into the house and then have a debate on it and use exactly the line of argument which the Minister of Trade and Commerce used last night. In other words, to suggest that there was the necessity for the greatest speed, and that they could not possibly have taken the time necessary to put through legislation to deal with the situation.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that no member of the house, and I am confident that no Canadian in the country, will fall into the trap which the Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to set last night. They say that in attacking the action of the government in passing this order in council we are attempting to suggest that there is not the necessity of immediate and vigorous action to deal with the possibility of trade with communist China. Of course there is the necessity of immediate and vigorous action to deal with the situation. That necessity is not new; that necessity has existed for over a year. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has been pressing for over two years for legislation to be introduced dealing with the communist problem and the problem of trading with communist countries, and the government has steadfastly refused to introduce such legislation.
Under the guise of emergency, a disguise which is said to be used to dispel all opportunities of criticism, we have the argument that we had to deal with this thing speedily, and therefore an order in council passed under the Emergency Powers Act was the only way with which to deal with it. "Some time ago."

It was the wrong way to bring that matter in, by order in council, at a time when parliament was in session. It was the wrong way to bring that matter in iby order in council six weeks after the matter had been brought to the attention of the government by the officials of the United Kingdom parliament, six weeks after the government had the measure under consideration; and the only excuse the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gives, which he gave last night, is "We did it without too much debate. It was done promptly."
Now, Mr. Speaker, if that is to be the standard by which we are to judge the efficiency of parliament then let us have all government legislation done without too much debate and done promptly-by executive orders, which is exactly the way Stalin throughout his regime did things in Russia, and exactly the way in which Hitler in his regime did things in Germany. Why have a parliament at all if the criterion of success of that parliament is to be getting things done without too much debate and getting them done promptly? Certainly any cabinet, any government, can do things by executive order much more promptly than they can be done through the democratic processes of parliament.

Now, to get on with the story, I may say that Manitoba has decided to make this restitution; but in the meantime, following the law, Manitoba remitted to Ottawa 75 per cent of the money which had been collected from these living pensioners. This was in accordance with the law because the former old age pension under the means test was paid 75 per cent from the federal treasury and 25 per cent by the province. When there were any collections for overpayments, therefore, the amount collected had to be divided in that same proportion. It appears now that the Manitoba government has not yet been assured by Ottawa that Ottawa will return that 75 per cent.
That, Mr. Speaker, is my grievance. I am sorry it has taken quite so long to get to it, but I felt it was necessary to give the background so the house would understand it. Let it be clear that I think Manitoba was wrong in the first place because it collected this money, but Manitoba stopped collecting it because of the letter written to Mr. Bell by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on February 9.
