I know of no better way to demonstrate the clarity which the minister attributes to me than by quoting from his own letter. I find on page 4 of the letter of February 9, which he wrote to Mr. Bell, after the paragraph which I quoted a while ago, the following:
In the case of the other nine provinces-
That is, the other nine apart from Manitoba.
-this is exactly what happened,
That is, that in the case of the other nine they discontinued collecting these overpayments. I go on from the letter:
-and the statement which I made in reply to a question recently In the house is literally correct, namely, that no province with the single exception of Manitoba has been endeavouring to take further action on its own initiative with respect to the recovery of these overpayments. Since these lists have been furnished to us the federal government has recognized and accepted this position. It has not objected or written to any of these provinces to insist that they continue to make further efforts to recover these overpayments.
What does that mean, Mr. Speaker? It means that the federal department wrote to each of the provinces at the end of December, 1951, and said to them:	"You furnish
us with a list of the people who might owe any of this money, and let the matter rest there until some decision has been made." The other nine provinces took that as an indication that they need not collect any of this money that had been overpaid. Manitoba did not take it that way; but when Manitoba received this letter I think Manitoba was perfectly justified in feeling that they misunderstood the previous correspondence and that it was a mistake, shall I put it, on their part to have made these collections. If they were led to feel that it was a mistake on their part I think they did the right thing in deciding to refund that money. I also think Manitoba is perfectly justified in expecting Ottawa to return to Manitoba the 75 per cent of that $14,000 which in the meantime Manitoba had remitted to Ottawa.
If Ottawa is not prepared to remit that 75 per cent, look at the discrimination that results, emanating from Ottawa, as between living pensioners in one province and living pensioners in the other nine provinces of Canada. It would mean that roughly $10,000 would be in the federal treasury, collected from living pensioners in Manitoba on this basis; whereas there would be no such

money in the federal treasury collected on that basis from living pensioners in the other nine provinces of Canada.
Every time the minister has got up to interrupt me during the course of these remarks I dared to hope that he was going to take my speech away from me by stating that this issue had been settled favourably. I hoped the minister would say that negotiations between Ottawa and Manitoba on this point have now been concluded with the result that 75 per cent of that $14,000 will be refunded to Manitoba, so that Manitoba in turn can pass it back to these 385 pensioners in my province from whom this money was collected.
The case is unanswerable, Mr. Speaker. We are really amazed that there has been any delay on the part of the federal government in dealing with it in a fair and proper way. It has been a sorry story across these past 15 or 16 months, the way in which people who drew pensions under the former Old Age Pensions Act have been hounded by the ghost of a means test which supposedly died so far as those 70 and over are concerned on December 31, 1951. It is particularly annoying to me that this should be done with respect to older Canadians in only one province. It has also been annoying the way in which this has been tossed back and forth between provincial and federal governments.
I think both governments have been to blame. I certainly do not give the Manitoba government a clean bill of health in this matter. I feel that long ago they should have interpreted that letter, the one back at the end of 1951, in the same way the other nine provinces did; but they did not do it that way. Since they made the mistake of collecting the money, they had to be brought to time in the way I have indicated.
It seems to me that this government should now put this matter on an even keel across the country by refunding the money that Manitoba sent to Ottawa, so they can give back in full what they collected from these 385 pensioners and end this sorry story on a much more pleasant note than it has had up to this time.

Overpayments to Old Age Pensioners

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

speechtext:
Yes. Administration of that
act is left to the provinces, and if the provinces choose to collect overpayments that is something that flows from a responsibility that arises out of its assumption of the administration of the Old Age Pensions Act.
After the passage of the Old Age Security Act Manitoba continued to recover overpayments that had been made in connection with the Old Age Pensions Act. What my hon. friend is asking me to do is to accept the responsibility for the action of a province. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that is neither a fair suggestion, nor is it one that I can possibly accede to. The provinces administer this measure in accordance with agreements executed between Canada on the one hand and the provinces on the other.
My hon. friend referred to the letter I wrote to Mr. Bell on February 9. Since he has done so I think it should be placed on Hansard in its entirety to indicate what the situation is. While the letter is a little long, I propose to do that. On February 9 I wrote to the minister of health and public welfare in Manitoba as follows:
Dear Mr. Bell:
I have your letter of February 2 on the subject of overpayments under the former Old Age Pensions Act. I think there is a good deal of misunderstanding and confusion about this matter, arising in part at least out of the fact that a number of separate questions have at various times been under discussion and the subject of correspondence.
I note, for example, that in one of the Winnipeg papers for Tuesday, February 3, you are quoted as being "amazed" at what I said recently in the House of Commons in reply to a question on the subject of overpayments; and you are alleged to have indicated that it was the opposite of what I told you in letters written March 4 and April 8, 1952. If you will examine the text of those letters, you will see, I am sure, that nowhere did they refer to, touch upon or deal with the subject of overpayments at all. Those letters dealt rather with the subject of recoveries from estates and with the repeal of the Old Age Pensions Act. They were written in reply to letters directed to me by your predecessor Mr. Schultz under dates of February 20, March 11 and March 15; and once again, if you will examine those letters and the resolution of the Manitoba legislature which prompted Mr. Schultz to write me on those occasions, you will see that Mr. Schultz' letters and the resolution passed by the Manitoba legislature dealt similarly with the questions of recoveries from estates and the repeal of the Old Age Pensions Act, and that, in fact, the resolution passed by the Manitoba legislature specifically excluded the question of recovery of overpayments from the subject matter of its recommendation.
I have carefully reviewed all the correspondence that has passed between this department and your department on the subject of overpayments, and

Overpayments to Old Age Pensioners
so far as I have been able to discover, this subject, as distinct from recoveries from estates and the question of the repeal of the Old Age Pensions Act, has never been dealt with at any time in correspondence between Mr. Schultz, your predecessor and myself. Most of the correspondence between our two departments has dealt with the questions of the repeal of the act and recoveries from estates, and very little has been directed to the question of overpayments.
I note, however, that in a letter dated January 3, 1952, my deputy, Dr. Davidson, wrote to your Mr. McNeill-as he did to the corresponding officials of all provincial governments-setting forth the legal position and advising as to the attitude of the federal government on the subject of overpayments. In that letter, it was pointed out that, so far as the legal position goes,-
And I think it is important to emphasize this.
-overpayments are technically and legally debts owing by the pensioner to the provincial government, and that consequently the collection of them was basically a provincial responsibility. It was pointed out further that the Old Age Pensions Act had not been repealed, and that the legal position of the provinces with respect to the recovery of overpayments was therefore the same as it had always been, and that this would continue to be the case until the actual repeal of the Old Age Pensions Act.
Having thus outlined the legal position, Dr. Davidson then went on to point out that the means by which the provincial pension authorities had traditionally endeavoured to recover overpayments,-namely, suspension of pension or partial reduction,-would no longer be available to them after December 31, 1951, when pensioners were transferred to the new Old Age Security Act. In recognition of this fact, the federal government had included a provision in its Financial Administration Act, which made it possible under certain circumstances for the federal authorities to take over from the provinces the responsibility of further recoveries by way of deduction from federal payments such as old age security. In consequence of the passage of this new legislation, Dr. Davidson requested the provincial authorities in Manitoba and in the other provinces to undertake the preparation of lists of all outstanding overpayments as at December 31, 1951. He further indicated that if these lists could be prepared on the basis of certain detailed information which he outlined in his letter, it would facilitate the task of the federal authorities and, in the final instance, of the federal treasury board in determining the steps which the federal government should take under section 95(3) of the Financial Administration Act to effect recovery of these overpayments.
I have dealt in some detail with the contents of this letter of January 3, 1952, because, so far as I can determine, it is the only letter which has ever dealt in any detail with the position of the federal government respecting overpayments. An identical letter was sent under the same date to each of the provincial pension authorities. In every case without exception, the provincial authorities complied with the request that lists of overpayments should be prepared and furnished to us. In the case of two provinces, these lists are not yet complete, but despite that, I think it can be fairly said that all the provinces complied substantially with our request.

And I add, in parentheses, pursuant to its legal obligations under section 95 (3) of the Financial Administration Act.
-or the further action, if any, which the federal government might wish to suggest that the provinces themselves should take.
In the case of the other nine provinces, this is exactly what happened, and the statement which I made in reply to a question recently in the house is literally correct,-namely, that no province with the single exception of Manitoba has been endeavouring to take further action on its own initiative with respect to the recovery of these overpayments since these lists have been furnished to us. The federal government has recognized and accepted this position. It has not objected or written to any of these provinces to insist that they continue to make further efforts to recover these overpayments.
And I add again, by way of parenthesis: For the simple reason that it had no authority to do so. Any policy of seeking overpayments is a matter that is dependent entirely upon the competence and the authority with which the provincial government itself has endowed itself. Then the letter continues:
We have not insisted or pressed the provinces to make further efforts to recover these overpayments because we recognize that with the transfer of these pensioners to the old age security rolls, the provinces are no longer in touch with the individuals concerned and consequently have not the facilities which they formerly possessed for the effective recovery of the amounts which have been overpaid.
But while the federal government accepts this position, it remains true that the Old Age Pensions Act is still in existence,-
Again, by way of parenthesis, I must emphasize that it is still in existence. It is the law of the land; and no minister or any combination of members from this side of the house or from the other side has any power to halt the operation of something that is still the law of the land. Then, to repeat the first part of this paragraph:
But while the federal government accepts this position, it remains true that the Old Age Pensions Act is still in existence, and that the technical legal obligations resting upon the provincial authorities in connection with this legislation remain essentially as they were before the act ceased to be operative. This being the case, you will readily understand, I am sure, why it is not possible for me, as the minister charged with the responsibility for administering the act, to direct an instruction or even a request to any provincial authority asking or authorizing it to disregard what are undoubtedly its legal obligations under the act. As I said in another connection in my

letter of March 4, 1952, to your predecessor Mr. Schultz, "we have not told the provinces that they should or that they should not continue to make recoveries from estates". Likewise, we have not told the provinces that they should or that they should not continue to make further efforts to recover overpayments. All that we can do is to point out the legal position as it now exists and as it will continue to exist until a proclamation is issued by the governor in council setting the date for the repeal of the Old Age Pensions Act in accordance with section 13 (2) of the Old Age Security Act.
Having thus set forth what is undoubtedly the technical legal position, I must say that I do not feel called upon in my capacity as the responsible federal minister to do more than that. It is then for each province to decide on its own initiative what it wishes to do or what it will do in this matter of overpayments. Nine provinces have taken no further steps to recover overpayments due to them since they submitted their lists as requested in the early part of 1952. I have not objected to that course of action in the case of any province.
And I might have added that I would have had no authority to do so.
The province of Manitoba has exercised its undoubted right (since these overpayments are technically and legally debts due to the crown in the right of the province of Manitoba) to make further attempts to recover these overpayments. That again is undoubtedly the right of the province of Manitoba, and I have had no quarrel with that either. All that I have said-and this continues to be my position-is that while such collections are undoubtedly made in conformity with the federal law (i.e. the regulations and the agreement made under the law), these overpayments are legally a matter for the provincial government, since they are without question debts owed to the province and not to the federal government.
With this explanation, I trust it will be possible for the Manitoba authorities to come to a satisfactory decision as to their future policy with respect to the recovery of overpayments.
I should add, in fairness, that when I made the statement in the house that Manitoba was the only province, naturally I acted upon information I was given. I find, however, that my statement was not entirely correct, and that there had been some smaller payments made in at least some provinces. I wrote to Mr. Bell and pointed that out to him, as I now point it out to the house. I think the correspondence gives the details.

It has been stated that the authorities there are going to make these repayments, but it is not at all clear whether or not they are going to undertake to pay the 75 per cent which was turned over to the federal authorities when they collected it.
Having regard to the uncertain position in which this matter was left at the end of 1951 as between the minister and the provincial government of Manitoba, I would think thei e is some obligation on the federal government to reimburse these people. The minister sa; s we are speaking for the provincial treasure, but my concern is that the recipients then -selves be reimbursed. Whether it be through

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the estimates of this department afford an opportunity of reviewing the trade position of the country. In his speech last Friday evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce reviewed this subject as he sees it and also made some comments on the condition of internal trade in Canada following the lines of the budget speech made by his colleague, the Minister of Finance, some two months ago. It is to be observed that the estimates of the department this year amount to $17,316,971, an increase of approximately $400,000 over those of the previous year.
The approach of the official opposition to this matter is based upon a recognition of the fundamental importance to Canada of her export trade. Indeed, in a very real sense the maintenance of our markets abroad and the maintenance of a high and profitable standard of export trade is of the lifeblood of this country. We have been competing with France for the last several years for third position among the trading nations of the world. On a per capita basis our exports in 1952 amounted to approximately $575. In this respect we can compare the United States, whose per capita exports amounted to $170. On a per capita basis we are practically three and a half times their figure, and we are nearly double the per capita figure of the United Kingdom. Indeed, on a per capita basis we export less only than Hong Kong and New Zealand. Last year a quarter of our gross national production went to the export market.
I mention these facts to emphasize the extent of Canada's dependence upon healthy export markets for the maintenance of a strong Canadian economy. We were happy
Supply-Trade and Commerce indeed to see that the figures reflected that in the year 1952 our exports did expand and Canada's external trade reached the highest figure in her history. But, Mr. Chairman, we must not be led by contemplation of these figures into assuming that all is well with Canada's trading outlook, or that we can afford to sit back and be complacent in the face of certain hard facts. There was not much indication in the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce last Friday evening that some of these facts have received that recognition on the part of the government which I think they should receive. Some of the figures, while they look very good and are indeed a matter of gratification to us all, nevertheless bring little comfort to some sections of the Canadian economy.
The weakness in Canada's trading position at the present time, if one may sum it up in a sentence, lies in the loss of our markets for many of our agricultural products abroad, and principally the loss of the United Kingdom market, the traditional market for many of our agricultural products. Today we are selling no cheese to the United Kingdom for the first time in our history. We are selling hardly any bacon, pork, poultry, eggs, milk, beef, apples, fish and other food products. The loss of these markets has been a very serious challenge to the well-being of the Canadian economy. We are faced with a great surplus of pork in Canada. Figures have been given of 100 million pounds, with 40 million of it in the form of canned pork on hand. This surplus exerts a heavy pressure on our market, on the prices our farmers are receiving for their products.
These are all the direct result of the loss of the United Kingdom market for these important agricultural products. The problem is, how shall these markets be recovered? The Minister of Trade and Commerce in his speech on April 17 did not seem to be unduly concerned. In fact it would be correct to say that he did not display any particular concern over the loss of these markets; for in characteristic fashion, he summed up the situation at page 4063 of Hansard in these words:
The simplest way I can describe the present economic situation in Canada is to say that at no time in the past have Canadians been more prosperous.
Well, Mr. Chairman, let the Minister of Trade and Commerce say that to some of the farmers of this country. The minister undertook to tell the house also that the government has done everything possible to recover our traditional markets, by which I assume

Supply-Trade and Commerce he meant the markets for our agricultural surplus in the United Kingdom. Mr. Chairman, it will take a great deal more than that mere assertion on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to convince the people of this country, and particularly the farmers of this country, that the government has done everything possible to recover our traditional markets. Perhaps, however, we may recognize this change of attitude shown in the minister's statement. He is at least recognizing the fact that the country under this present administration has lost those traditional markets. Hitherto we have been hearing only airy and confident statements from the treasury benches to the effect that things were never so good in the country before. Well, tell that to the farmers who have lost their traditional markets for bacon, pork, poultry, eggs, milk, cheese, fish and other products.
Let us have a look at some of the figures issued by the minister's own department on this subject. I have the dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin for February 10, from which I read:
Accrued net income of farm operators from farm production declined by $255 million in 1952, a drop of 12 per cent from the record level established in 1951. This decline is largely attributable to a severe drop in livestock prices of between 20 and 25 per cent, and a 10 per cent rise in farm operating expenses. The record wheat crop of 688 million bushels was of excellent grade, and initial prices were unchanged; but these factors were not sufficient to offset the developments mentioned above.

Yes, foot-and-mouth disease did enter into what happened to the prices for livestock in this country, but that is not the whole story. These markets have been lost, and we are not satisfied that this government has made the resolute efforts required to recover them. The government has shown too characteristic an attitude of sitting back and viewing everything with complacency.
The government are making much of the fact that they were represented at the prime ministers' conference last autumn. Well, Mr. Chairman, it is to be remembered that we waited a good many years for this conference to be called before any steps were taken in that direction, and all the while our markets in the United Kingdom and abroad for our agricultural products were contracting. Yet when we brought the matter up in the house it was turned down every time. On October 21, 1949, as found in Hansard at page 1023, we moved for the calling of a conference of the nations of the commonwealth "for the purpose of working out arrangements to preserve and enlarge those traditional markets on which jobs and 
opportunities for Canadians very largely depend". What was the fate of that proposal put forward in the interests of the Canadian agricultural producers? It was defeated, Mr. Chairman, by the Liberal majority in this house. They voted solidly against it.
Let us come down to 1950, when a similar motion was introduced on behalf of the official opposition in this house. On February 28, 1950, as recorded at page 308 of Hansard, this amendment was moved:
this house is of the opinion that the government should take immediate steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth and the countries of the empire to devise policies to restore our lost markets, and thereby to provide jobs for our Canadian people.
What was the fate of that proposal? The same fate, Mr. Chairman; it was defeated by the Liberal majority in this house, with every Liberal in the house voting against the proposal.
Coming down to 1952, on June 3 of that year the Leader of the Opposition moved this amendment:
this house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currencies, and to explore all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends. [DOT]
What was the fate of that motion? The same as that of the others; it was defeated in this house by the Liberal majority, with every Liberal voting against it.
Of course, Mr. Chairman, great virtue is claimed for the fact that the government was represented at the prime ministers' conference in London in December. While we are glad to have seen Canada represented there, we have not forgotten that the effectiveness of such a conference would have been much greater if it had been called long before; and it was not called long before because this government decided against it. The conference of last December was belated. The government went into that conference with a lack of enthusiasm, as reflected in its attitude in the house on the occasions to which I have referred.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word on the subject of wheat. It is a matter of very great satisfaction indeed that while our exports to the United Kingdom of other agricultural products were declining, and indeed were being cut off entirely, our exports of wheat to the United Kingdom did increase substantially in 1952. Indeed, our exports of wheat moved up approximately 40 per cent in value, from $441 million in 1951 to $621 million in 1952.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE

No; an increase of something like 40 per cent. Our flour exports to the United Kingdom rose just slightly. But, Mr. Chairman, lest we sit back on our oars let us remember that even taking account of the increase in 1952 in exports of wheat to the United Kingdom over 1951, nevertheless the total of such exports was not sufficient to make up, as is pointed out in the quotation I read from the dominion bureau of statistics bulletin, for what the farmers in this country have suffered through loss of income from other products.
In this year, 1953, we have more wheat to sell than ever before. Indeed, the big carryover in this country presents a serious problem. The dominion bureau of statistics daily bulletin of April 13 puts the problem in this way:
Supplies of wheat remaining on or about March 1 this year in the four major wheat exporting countries-United States, Canada, Argentina, and Australia-for export and carryover at the end of their respective crop years amounted to 1,468,200,000 bushels, some 66 per cent greater than the 885,600,000 available a year ago, according to the March issue of the bureau's wheat review.
Supplies on March 1 this year (in millions of bushels) were as follows, with last year's figures in brackets: United States, 668-2 (411-6); Canada, 533-3 ( 391-2); Argentina, 160-3 (2-1); and Australia, 106-4 (80-7).
So, Mr. Chairman, you can see at a glance that in every one of those four exporting countries the carryover of wheat is substantially greater than a year ago. This bulletin proceeds:
Exports of Canadian wheat as grain in February amounted to 14,000,000 bushels, the lowest monthly total for the current crop year, states the bureau's wheat review. Wheat shipments during February may normally be expected to be lower than those of other winter months, but an additional factor this year was the strike of elevator workers at several of the larger west coast terminals normally handling a substantial share of the export movement. Although this year's February wheat exports were some 4,700,000 bushels lower than in January and 4,600,000 below those of February 1952, they were 3,800,000 greater than in February, 1951.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we are soon to have in this house a debate on the new international wheat agreement, and I do not intend to attempt to anticipate that debate or the course of it. However, before I leave this subject of wheat after commenting on the effect of this big carryover and the problem that it presents for the whole Canadian economy, I must comment that it must be a matter of disappointment to all Canadians that the United Kingdom has not seen fit to subscribe to the wheat agreement.
This agreement is of very great importance to Canada. The assurance of a market for our wheat is of the most vital importance, not
Supply-Trade and Commerce only to the agricultural economy of this country but to the whole national economy. We have only to think of what happened several months ago to recognize the danger that would confront the economy of this country if the United Kingdom should transfer to Russia or other countries, for instance, even a substantial portion of her wheat purchases. We had an example in January last in the scare that was created when a report was issued that Great Britain was turning to Russia for the purchase of 600,000 tons of wheat. The scare which resulted is just an example of the feeling of concern we must have in this country for the whole future of the marketing of our wheat. An agreement without Britain subscribing, when she is the leading wheat importer in the world and particularly for Canada, is after all something like the play without Hamlet.
The United Kingdom market for our wheat is fundamental to our national prosperity. Whatever may be the reasons which have led the United Kingdom government to their decision not to adhere to this agreement, whether it be that the maximum price of $2.05 was 5 cents more than they wished to pay or whether it was some antagonism toward bulk buying, nevertheless it is a matter of very great concern indeed to all Canadians.
I have not time at this stage, Mr. Chairman, to say as much as I wished to say on the subject of raw materials and the extent to which Canada could strengthen her economy by the greater processing of raw materials at home. The economy of this country has been immensely strengthened by the extent to which we are now able to draw upon domestic sources for oil, which used to be a major import from the United States. Notwithstanding discoveries of vast ore bodies in Canada, iron and its products still remain a major factor in the import situation in this country. In 1952 our imports of iron and its products from all countries amounted to $1,407 million, of which we purchased only $122 million from the United Kingdom and $1,231 million from the United States.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word concerning our trading relations with the United States. Geography has dictated that our trading relations with the United States shall always be intimate. Political factors oftentimes have had a contrary influence. In the past three years, 1950, 1951 and 1952, our imports from the United States rose in both amount and percentage. Our exports to the United States in 1952 were approximately the same in value as in 1951, while the percentage they represented of the total of Canadian exports dropped from 59 per cent to 54 per cent, and in the first two months of this year our exports remained stable.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
There is a feature of our trading position with the United States which is not new. In 1950 our import 'balance in trade with the United States, as it is now euphoniously called, was just $80 million; in 1951 it increased to $479 million, and in 1952 to $628 million. This is a continuing problem for the Canadian economy, the extent to which we are confronted with an import balance in our trading relations with the United States. It is quite true that the United States is our best customer, but we are her best customer. The difference in amount, Mr. Chairman, is something that is fundamental in our whole trading position. It is the danger that results from a country placing most of its trading eggs in one basket.
In the case of the United States, in 1952 she took 54 per cent of our exports and supplied us with 74 per cent of our imports. In other words, Mr. Chairman, 64 per cent of this country's trade, export and import, with the world was done with one country, the United States. While our political and economic relationships with the United States may be on the whole very satisfactory, and on the political side are certainly an inspiration to the world, nevertheless there are very great economic dangers in this condition of unbalance between exports and imports. Indeed, the Minister of National Revenue recognized this, for he is reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of September 12, 1952 in these words:
Canada's economic position, at present strong, also has a weakness, Revenue Minister McCann told the National Tax Association at its 45th annual conference in the Royal York Hotel yesterday.
"That weakness is that Canada depends so much upon the United States," said Dr. McCann. "Canadians can never be freed from the fear of a slump in the U.S., for which we would not in any way be responsible and which we could do little to control."
There is a commendable recognition of the problem. It is a continuing problem of serious proportions when we measure the strength of our trading position. Wherever we may expand our exports -to the United States, let us bear in mind that that is no adequate substitute for the loss of markets in the United Kingdom, because of the fact that the purchases made by the United States in such cases are not of the same products as those which Great Britain had been accustomed to make in the past before we lost our traditional markets there.
Now, what of our trading relations with the United States? What is to be said of some of the more pressing problems that confront us there? We are waiting to see, of course, what will be the effective trading policy of the new congress, not just the new administration, but the new congress. We recall that Senator Taft has said, as reported 
in a Reuters dispatch of November 18, that he doubted whether U.S. tariffs could be reduced much further. Again Mr. Taft said that U.S. tariffs had been reduced to their lowest point already, and he added:
I personally doubt if changes in tariffs would result in any substantial increase of imports into the United States.
President Eisenhower has made statements which, on the whole, contribute to a feeling of confidence in this country, but whether or not that policy will be reflected in the United States congress is yet to be proven. There is pressing need, Mr. Chairman, so far as our trading relations with the United States are concerned, for customs simplification. Legislation for that purpose was urged upon congress by President Eisenhower. It is a fact that the authority of collectors of customs in United States ports is very broad. There is so much uncertainty and so many differences in the way these customs regulations are applied that they have created very serious problems for Canadian producers seeking to export to the United States. We would have liked to hear more from the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to efforts on the part of this government to seek the enactment of such a measure on the part of a friendly United States administration.
Then there is that problem, Mr. Chairman, which is of quite serious concern to the Canadian farmers, particularly the Canadian dairy farmers. The deliberate breach of the provisions of GATT by the United States congress in the face of protests on the part of the administration, both in the days of President Truman and since the time of President Eisenhower within quite recent months, has not only had the effect of excluding Canadian dairy products on a large scale, but has given rise to feelings of disquiet and uncertainty as to the whole future of our relations with the United States under the general agreement on tariffs and trade. It has hurt the Canadian dairy producer, and it has challenged the whole principle of these agreements.
I should like to say a word concerning our trading relations with the United Kingdom. I have mentioned already the loss of that traditional market for virtually all of our agricultural products except wheat and flour. Salmon is another product that we used to ship in large quantities to the United Kingdom. Apart from an altogether too small order that was announced recently by the Minister of Fisheries, the market for our salmon in the United Kingdom has been greatly reduced and virtually lost. Again, the United Kingdom used to take great quantities of our timber exports. That market has

been greatly contracted, and the timber producers of this country are suffering accordingly.
It is true that our exports to the United Kingdom in the years 1950, 1951 and 1952 rose in amount though not in percentage, while-and this is regrettable-our imports from the United Kingdom declined in those three years drastically in both amount and percentage of our total. With the financial and trading difficulties which confront the United Kingdom, Mr. Chairman, it is evident that the United Kingdom must have access to more dollars if she is going to be able to increase her purchases from this country. I realize the Canadian government cannot do everything in this respect. To be fair, I would be the first to recognize that fact. But I hope we can make more rapid progress toward the St. Lawrence waterway, because there is an opportunity opening up for Great Britain to increase her sale of heavy equipment with accompanying engineering services in this country.
In his review last Friday night the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not tell us anything about purchases from the United Kingdom on government account. We wish to see the purchases this country is making for national defence used as a means of strengthening our trade with the United Kingdom; for if these purchases that we have to make abroad are routed to the United Kingdom, then the United Kingdom is correspondingly going to have more dollars with which to purchase our agricultural products, and that is highly necessary at the present time.
These facts are recognized in the United Kingdom, because when the overseas trade minister, Mr. Harry Mackeson, left London last September to visit Canada and the United States with a view to increasing the export of United Kingdom products to these dollar countries we read in a Reuters dispatch that he said this:
"But it is mainly in the field of capital equipment, plant and machinery, that we can expect to increase our exports", he said.
That is their exports to Canada and the United States.
Britain is best able to meet competition from other countries in the engineering field, where she can exploit her skill and experience in specialized work such as electrical engineering, machine tools and prefabricated buildings for export, he said.
I hoped that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might hold out some hope to us of enlargement of the token import scheme which has been in effect in the United Kingdom in this post-war period. Forty per cent of the basic period was the maximum permitted in certain imports laid down in that 68108-269
Supply-Trade and Commerce token scheme. In January, 1952, even this percentage suffered a 25 per cent reduction, so that in this scheme only 30 per cent of the United Kingdom imports in the basic pre-war period of 1936 to 1939 is being permitted to enter the United Kingdom.
The minister has said much about our trade with Latin America. It is true that our exports to Latin America in the years 1950, 1951 and 1952 rose in amount and percentage. In the same years our imports showed a slight rise. In 1952 our exports to and imports from Latin America were in almost complete balance. However, our exports to Latin America have fallen off sharply in 1953, partly as a result of reduced shipments of automobiles, and our imports from Latin America in 1953 thus far are also slightly lower. I am not going to say, of course, Mr. Chairman, that that has anything to do with the visit of the Minister of Trade and Commerce this year to Latin America, but it does emphasize that we must make every effort to take advantage of the trading opportunities that lie in the Latin American market.
As to our position with respect to Europe, Mr. Chairman, in these three years, 1950, 1951 and 1952, our exports to Europe showed a substantial and gratifying increase in amount and percentage. But in the first two months of 1953 they dropped by one-third as compared with the first two months of 1952, and that is a very serious decline. We hope that it will be arrested. Our imports from Europe in 1952 declined both in percentage and amount. The increase in strength of the German economy augurs well for this country, if we can continue to find in Germany a market for our wheat.
In his review the minister said very little about trade with countries behind the iron curtain. We are still doing some trade with most of those countries. It was reported last November that the Canadian government was taking steps to restrain dumping in this country on the part of two of the countries behind the iron curtain, Czechoslovakia and Poland, but we have heard very little on that subject since. I hope we may hear what steps the government is taking in dealing with the problem of dumping in the Canadian market by countries behind the iron curtain.
The minister had some words to offer to the house concerning the general agreement on tariffs and trade. We are greatly concerned about the continuance of this agreement on tariffs and trade. Unquestionably, Mr. Chairman, while there are two sides to the ledger with respect to GATT, nevertheless it was an important achievement when, in 1947, 34 countries entered into general

Supply-Trade and Commerce agreements on tariffs and trade, and when it was possible to extend these agreements as a result of the subsequent conferences at Torquay and Annecy. The continuance of these agreements is not to be assumed. Therefore, since the trading outlook of this country depends to a very substantial extent on the continuation of these general agreements on tariffs and trade, we hope the government will lose no opportunity to put its whole strength and weight behind efforts which may be made to extend these agreements.
It is a fact, of course, that the future of GATT, particularly in reference to Canada, depends to a considerable degree upon the extent to which the United States will give willing subscription to the extension of these agreements. President Eisenhower himself has declared for their extension; but it remains to be seen what attitude the congress will take, particularly in the light of the action of congress, in breach of GATT, in imposing the ban on imports into that country of dairy products from Canada and other countries that are parties to GATT.
In his review the minister did not have anything to say concerning the problem of the convertibility of currency. This is a problem of very great proportions. I should be the last to underestimate the difficulties involved; but we must do all we can in concerting efforts with the United Kingdom and other countries of the sterling bloc to revive convertibility, at least initially, on some current basis. The problems are very great; but there will not be any lasting solution of our trading problems with them, and there will be a continued loss of markets in the United Kingdom, unless this problem is grappled with and eventually a solution found for it.
Therefore, summing the matter up in conclusion, I should like to say that we in this part of the house do not view Canada's trading outlook with pessimism, far from it. On the other hand we do not view it as something the health of which can be regarded as assured for all time. On the contrary, I think what we need in our approach to this question is a realistic attitude, appreciating the strength of our trading position and also recognizing such weaknesses as have developed in it.
I mention these weaknesses as problems to which we should be alive, and which should attract our best efforts in seeking their solution. I do not purport necessarily to list them all in order of importance, but certainly I would put in first position the restoration of our lost markets, particularly in the United Kingdom, for our agricultural surplus;


Next, the future of our exports of wheat;
Next, the future of GATT, when the present agreements come to an end this year;
Next, the problem of having our trading eggs, to a dangerous degree, in one basket, and thereby emphasizing the desirability of our making a supreme, a herculean effort, to recover those markets in Great Britain and in other countries abroad for our agricultural products;
Next, the problem of doing what we may, and to encourage the United Kingdom and other members of the sterling bloc to do what they can, to restore the convertibility of currency as soon as that may be possible;
Next, the need of a greater degree of balance in our exports and imports in trading with the United States.
Next, there is also the problem which is presented by the re-emergence of Japan as a world trader. Up to this time we have not felt seriously the impact of post-war Japanese competition, but that is a problem we must prepare to meet. Japan is knocking on the door of GATT; and if she is admitted I do urge that something will be required from the Japanese government by way of an undertaking to conform to fair trading practices. Of necessity we must do something like that if Japan is to be admitted to the company of countries which are members of GATT, having regard to the experience we have had with Japanese dumping in pre-war years.
Finally, so far as this Progressive Conservative party is concerned, let me make it abundantly clear that our aim is not to restrict trade but rather to expand it. What I have said has been designed to stress the importance we attach to the maintenance and the expansion of our export trade. We want none of the smugness that has long been evident on the part of this government in the face of the loss of our traditional markets, and particularly the markets for our agricultural surpluses.
This is a matter of leading importance to Canada and, so far as the Progressive Conservative party is concerned, we regard it as something which must be a first national objective.
Trade is a two-way street. We cannot be satisfied simply with the trading position we hold today, strong though it may be in many respects. Our production is growing. It must continue to grow. We cannot take for granted even the continuance of our present markets. We must maintain those markets and must seek to expand them. We must seek further markets abroad. In all cases we must follow active policies. We must look ahead. And any thought that the free world should con-

tinue to be divided even partially into two trading blocs, dollar and sterling, is inconceivable to this country. If it were left that way it would spell very serious difficulty for our Canadian trading outlook.
No; Canadians in the years ahead will need to be efficient producers and efficient salesmen. In the export markets of the world we will have to meet competition that will be very keen. No doubt we will be confronted with challenges to keep down costs. We hope the government will contribute to lessening the costs of production by following a policy of reduced taxation, and that the whole Canadian economy will then be geared to a policy of expanding production and expanding sales abroad.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is the kind of debate in which I believe all members of the House of Commons are interested. Whatever may be our differences in approach to the problem of trade and commerce, we are all anxious to see this country prosper, to see our trading relationships bring to this country a high degree of welfare for our Canadian people, and to make our contribution to a better world.
We are a country that is peculiarly vulnerable economically, because of our dependence upon external markets. No one in his senses suggests that Canada can be made selfsufficient. We are not organized in that way. Our whole economy has been geared to supplying our own people with certain of their requirements, and producing vast quantities of certain commodities that by no conceivable stretch of the imagination could be consumed by ourselves. Therefore we must export our surplus in exchange for goods and services our people can use for their own benefit.
Canada is more dependent upon external trade than any other country in the world. For example, on a per capita basis we are the leading world trader. In absolute terms we have become, since the end of world war II, with the exception of one year, the number three trader. That one year was 1951.
This shows our dependency upon world trade, when we realize that, per head of population, we are first; and in absolute terms, with the exception of 1951, third. The United States and the United Kingdom have ranked first and second in absolute terms during these years, and it was in 1951 that France displaced Canada, and moved into the third position. As far as I have been able to see from the complete records for the first quarter of 1952 we have jumped to third position again, and from the present patterns of trade I think it is indicated that we are likely to maintain that place in the near future.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I believe that is all the more significant because we must realize that if we are to continue to expand as we have during the past few years, when our expansion has been very great indeed, exports must not only be as great as they are today but they must increase in proportion to our total production.
Let us look at the two leading items of export, newsprint and wheat. The foreign market for these particular commodities is very critical and always susceptible to factors beyond our control. For example, newsprint, wood pulp and pulpwood sales are dependent upon a high level of business activity in the United States. Some people may say that perhaps if that high level of activity in that great country were lessened we might be able to conserve our forest resources to a greater extent. I think that is true, especially when I see some of these United States papers, particularly the Sunday editions, and realize the number of Canadian trees that have gone into their production. I realize then how necessary it is for us to have some sort of forest conservation policy.
Nonetheless our economy is largely dependent upon our exports of newsprint and pulpwood to the United States. At the least sign of a recession advertising will drop, and with a drop in advertising the demand for our newsprint and pulpwood will drop because newspapers will be reduced in size to that extent. At the same time the Canadian producers would be forced to reduce their production of these commodities accordingly.
In connection with wheat we all realize in this house, particularly those of us who come from the prairie provinces, that a major factor in the production of wheat is the weather. As the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has said, most of us are greatly disturbed over the recent failure to effect an international wheat agreement. Under such an agreement at least we were assured of a major share of the United Kingdom market. We have not that assurance now. I suppose the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) may say, and quite correctly, that in any event the British will have to buy large quantities of Canadian wheat, but we have not the comfortable assurance today that we had under the international wheat agreement.
I regard with a good deal of misgiving any return to the uncertainties of the open market, especially with the increasing surpluses we have witnessed over the past year or two. Perhaps this should not have been unforeseen. I remember some of the debates that took place in the British house on the British wheat agreement which I think on the whole
