Supply-Trade and Commerce was of benefit to our western growers. Criticism of that agreement came from the ranks of the supporters of the government now in power in Great Britain. I will not say all of them, but I think many of them rather dislike negotiated agreements of this description and would be quite glad to see the Liverpool exchange opened again and have trading on the pre-war basis.
Last week I noticed in the United States paper a report which is quite serious to those of us who come from western Canada, and should be of serious concern to Canadians generally. The suggestion was made and apparently received sympathetically that an embargo should be placed upon the importation into the United States of coarse grains. In the representations that were made in Washington, Canada was mentioned particularly.
A serious curtailment of our exports to the United States and elsewhere of wheat, wood pulp, newsprint, coarse grains and other products would have a serious effect upon our whole economy. In 1952 wheat and newsprint-I am going to speak in very round numbers-each provided more than 20 per cent of our exports. It was a little more than 20 per cent in one case and a little less in the other, but together the exports of newsprint and wheat made up some 40 per cent of our total exports.
Let us look for a moment at another aspect of our external trade. In 1952 we imported fuel goods, that is coal, petroleum and its products, worth nearly $500 million. Nearly half a billion dollars worth of our imports in 1952 were fuel. Of course we hope that as time passes and new oil and gas fields are found and developed in western Canada we shall become more and more self-supplying in that regard. There is every indication that that will be so.
Then we are forced to import large quantities of rubber and bauxite to supply two of the great essential industries in this country. We have the Polymer plant owned and operated by the government. I once complimented the minister upon the Polymer plant as an example of public enterprise and I remember he said, perhaps with a good deal of pride, that it was not a public enterprise, it was his enterprise. I do not care whose enterprise it is, the Polymer plant has filled an important place in our economy. I hope under public enterprise it will continue to do so. But we still have to import raw rubber.
Of course we have to import bauxite for our huge aluminum industry. Our dependence upon imports becomes clear when it is noted that last year we brought in $1-25
[Mr. Coldwell.l

billion worth of capital goods which were required for our further expansion. These were made up of farm and non-farm machinery, automobile parts, rolling mill products, engines and boilers, aircraft parts, electrical apparatus and so on.
When we discuss these trade problems, our huge imports, our necessity for export markets and the necessity to balance our trade as far as we are able to do so, we also have to bear in mind that in spite of our huge production we have a relatively small population. The maintenance and raising of our standard of living, in view of our very limited population and domestic consumption, must be related to the sale of much of our production in external markets. When we export we do so primarily to import something that we can use or that will be beneficial to the people in this country, whether it be capital goods, consumable supplies or services that our people can use.
It is quite clear that our own consumers are not sufficient in number to purchase a large proportion of our domestic production. There is a limit to the amount of wheat that an individual can consume or the amount of newsprint or other products such as salmon, fish or bacon and pork. So we must continue to view with a great deal of interest our export markets. I think that is illustrated by the disposition of our two major products, newsprint and wheat. We are already among the leading consumers of both newsprint and wheat, but we must still largely depend upon foreign markets for the consumption of most of what we produce in both of these commodities.
If we are to do this properly we must consider the financial position of Canada in relation to the rest of the world. Of course this relationship obviously must have an immense bearing on our trade, for in absolute terms-absolute terms, let us not forget-we are still a debtor nation, although our position greatly improved in that respect as the result of world war II. But in so far as most countries are concerned we are a creditor nation. Indeed, it is only toward the United States that we remain a debtor nation, and this of course is of great importance when trade with Europe and particularly our trade with the United Kingdom are under discussion. It means that there is a complete reversal from the old days in our financial relationships with the United Kingdom.
In the old days the United Kingdom was a creditor to us but now she is a debtor. This means that not merely does she need to export goods to us-I shall put it this way, although it is not quite accurate-equivalent in value to her imports from us, but she

must export goods considerably in excess of her imports if she is to retire her debts, invest in Canadian industries-and I think most Canadians welcome such investments- and at the same time achieve something of a balance of payments with us. That of course is involved in what my hon. friend called convertibility just now. After all, convertibility is not entirely a question of financial arrangement. It is really a question of trade, the exchange of goods, the flowing of goods in various directions and so on, so that as goods move currencies appear and you have a reasonable relationship between those currencies which enables you to bring about a system of convertibility.
Old-time multilateral trade seems to be gone, and at least for the present it does seem to be far beyond our reach. More and more, whether we like it or whether we do not like it, trade becomes a question of exchange, and already in many instances and between some countries it has become in effect a matter of barter. That is an attractive trade arrangement in some respects so far as Great Britain is concerned, because of the shortage of certain currencies, in making trade agreements with the Soviet union and other iron curtain countries. That is not a financial arrangement but a matter of the exchange of goods under what amounts in many respects to some system of barter.
I spoke of imports, but let us look at the trade picture more closely as it affects our external relationships. Go back a few years. At least 15 per cent of our imports in each of the years between 1920 and 1929 came from the United Kingdom, with a peak of 18-4 per cent attained in 1924 and a low of 15 per cent in 1929. From 1930 right through 1938 our minimum imports from the United Kingdom were 16 per cent in 1931 with a peak of 24-4 per cent in 1933. In other words, as the depression became worse we seemed to have a higher percentage of imports from the United Kingdom. -
But since the end of world war II in 1945 our peak in imports from the United Kingdom only reached 12-7 per cent in 1950, while our imports reached a low of 7-4 per cent in 1947. In 1952 our imports were slightly higher at 8-9 per cent, but one might almost say no higher. That is the picture as far as the United Kingdom is concerned. I agree with the hon. member for Eglinton that we have to think of trade with the United Kingdom because so far as our trading relations are concerned, I think we are more secure with that country than we are with the United States.
I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday about the refusal of the United States to consider a low tender for
Supply-Trade and Commerce ships from a Canadian company in exactly the same way that the United States refused to consider a tender from the English Electric Company for hydroelectric goods which was very greatly below the lowest American tender. The minister said what is perfectly true, and I have no quarrel with it, at page 4141 of Hansard:
-but whether the government of the United Kingdom is justified in protesting as to how the United States buys its electrical equipment X cannot say.
He said it was the privilege of the United States to decide what they would do in that respect, but it illustrates the point I want to make. It shows how uncertain our trading relations with the United States are. It is not a question of tariff policy. It is an embargo against tenders from the United Kingdom and an embargo against tenders from Canada. If the United States is going to continue that kind of policy, what use is GATT to>
us? What use to us is any other trading arrangement? I think many of us in the house are pretty disturbed at the manner in which the United States has failed to live up to the understandings and the agreements to which we committed ourselves at Geneva in 1947 and which we have fulfilled. I think that is tragic because the American people are such generous-hearted, fine people, so friendly and all the rest of it to ourselves and to the rest of the world. Yet as a nation and as a government they are unreliable and often shortsighted. It is dangerous for us to place all our eggs in the United States basket. That, I think, is the lesson we have yet to learn.
Let us look at the picture as to imports from the United States in the same period. It shows exactly the opposite trend. From 1920 through 1929 the lowest record of imports was 64-9 per cent in 1924 and the highest was 68-9 per cent in 1920, closely followed by 68-8 per cent in 1929. I am taking these figures from the official records of the department. From 1930 through 1938 the low was 54-2 per cent in 1933 and the high was 64-8 per cent in 1930. Since the end of world war II the low was 67-1 per cent in 1950 and the high was reached last year with 73-9 per cent.
You will notice the reverse trend during the depression. The percentage of British imports went up and the percentage of United States imports went down. Imports from the United Kingdom during the past seven years have been at a level of 6 to 7 per cent lower than they were during the 1920's, and imports from the United States have been at a level of 3 to 5 per cent higher for the comparative periods. I think the outstanding feature of
4258	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce these figures is the concentration of our trade with one country, and that one country the United States.
This is particularly significant when we consider the fact that we are a debtor nation toward the United States and a creditor nation toward the United Kingdom. If the roles were reversed the concentration of our trade would reflect a very much happier picture as far as our Canadian economy and the future of this country are concerned. As it is we are exceedingly susceptible to any economic changes that take place in the United States. If a major depression did take place in the United States-and I hope it will not come there-our economy which is so highly dependent on our trade with that country would undergo serious and-yes, I would go so far as to say-disastrous dislocation.
So I can say to the minister that I think every effort should be made by this country to find other export markets, and I welcomed the fact that the minister took a trip to South America. I hope he and others will take trips to other parts of the world in an endeavour to diversify our markets as quickly as possible even though, may I add, that should result in what seem to be some short-term losses and indeed some short-term trading disadvantages. Of course, since the acceptability of a policy of this description to private manufacturers and traders is unlikely, even though it is in their long-term interests, I think the onus is on the government to adopt some appropriate course of action, and I am going to say something about that.
Such a policy should take into account both imports and exports. In the short-term view the latter appear to be less important. We are exporting more and more goods, and we are obtaining better prices for them. The increase is due to the fact that there is such a demand for raw materials with which we can supply the world, particularly in view of the general re-armament that is going on all over the world. However, it is not merely a matter of disposing of our products today but rather, as far as possible, of ensuring that we shall still be selling them tomorrow and the day after. This can be assured, and I hope the minister agrees, only by developing new markets overseas.
Important as is diversification of our export markets, more pressing is the diversification of our import markets. For example, while 70 per cent of our total exports in 1952 went to the United States and the United Kingdom, an even greater percentage-73-9 per cent of our imports-came from one of those two


countries. I mean 73-9 per cent of our total imports, $2,977,000,000 out of a total of $4,030,500,000, came from one of the two, from the United States. To my mind it is already obvious that such a situation is undesirable from considerations which I have already mentioned and perhaps from other points of view which could be given by other hon. members of the house.
I shall state some of the reasons why I think it is undesirable. First of all it leaves Canadian prices too much the prey of external forces over which we have no control. Second, it leaves us with a deficit in our balance of payments with the one country to which we are habitually in debt. For example, in the years 1949, 1950 and 1951 respectively we paid to the United States $205 million, $260 million and $321 million in interest or dividends. Rather than continue a policy which adds to this interest deficit with the United States we should, if possible, be compensating by exporting to the United States more goods than we import. That would be the ideal position.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: May I ask how my hon. friend accounts for the strength of the Canadian dollar?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: How do I account for the strength of the Canadian dollar? I think the answer, although I am not a financial expert, is that the strength of the Canadian dollar is due to a very large extent to the demand for Canadian dollars for investment in our resources and industry, as well, of course, as the purchase of raw materials for defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: The balance of investments is against us.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Well, you asked me what I thought and I am giving what I think is the reason. If I am wrong I hope the minister will explain to the house why the Canadian dollar has been so strong over the past number of months. Well, if multilateral trade were operating effectively and the United States discontinued its policy of resisting imports, there would be an alternative means of balancing our payments through the free flow of United States dollars into other countries with which we have an excess of exports from Canada.
That is the old-fashioned way of settling balances of trade between nations. That has been for a number of years-and it will be for some time to come, if it ever returns again-far from the case. It is therefore necessary that we adopt the most effective methods to rectify all this. They in turn will help to alleviate the third undesirable feature, that of the present concentration

of our exports. The solution, I think, is to shift as many of our purchases as possible from the United States to other markets, particularly to the United Kingdom, to western Europe or indeed to other parts of the sterling area and, again, to South America. If we can direct our trade in those directions there will be a long-term gain and something of long-term insurance.
As a means of solving some of these problems I am going to summarize what I have said and perhaps expand on one or two points on which I have not already expanded. I think sterling might be accepted in part payment for Canadian produce sold to sterling area countries. You may say to me: what are we going to do with that sterling we accumulate as credits overseas? Well, sterling could be used to buy sterling area goods, or it could be used in sterling areas that are undeveloped and which we sometimes call underprivileged or backward countries. It could form part of our contribution to the Colombo plan and although I know that satisfactory arrangements might not be possible, but if it were possible I would like to see us use some of it for the technical aid projects of the United Nations. I want to say something about those technical aid projects and Canada's part in them when we return to the estimates of the Department of External Affairs.
Then we might have a much higher proportion of governmental orders for supplies placed in the sterling areas. I was looking over some of the orders that have been placed for equipment and supplies in the United Kingdom and the sterling area, and I was astounded at the relatively small amounts of supplies that are bought in the sterling area by Canada for our various projects and our various departments.
Of course we have tariffs and dumping duties on imports from Britain which we put into effect last year. We raised the tariff on textiles under the Geneva agreements in 1948, and certain dumping duties were applied against Britain on goods sold for less than their home market price. Those duties applied to automobiles and some other supplies sold in this country. I think the tariffs against countries with which we want to trade should be lowered to make it easier for those countries to earn Canadian dollars with which to buy Canadian products. That, of course, is of particular interest to those of us who are from the prairie provinces, where we have been so dependent up to the present time on the export of commodities which we produce there in large volume.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Then we should try to make long-term commodity agreements for specific imports and exports. It may be difficult to do that. As I said earlier, I think the present government in Great Britain does not like the idea of specific agreements of this nature. But there are other countries which might be inclined to enter into such agreements. In the position in which we find ourselves, perhaps we could make credit arrangements which would facilitate the conclusion of such agreements.
There is a matter which I have not discussed but which is very closely connected with the world wheat agreement; that is that Canada should give, and has not given, full support to the establishment of a world food pool very much along the lines suggested at the United Nations by Lord Boyd Orr. It was proposed to the FAO as well by the international federation of agriculture several years ago. While the idea was not immediately acceptable to the government, in view of our long-term interests I think Canada should give all the support possible to that proposal when it is made again before the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations.
Then I think there are certain emergency measures that might be adopted. An offer might be made to the British government for postponement for three years-I have made this suggestion several times before-of the interest on the annual payment to be made on the British loan, providing the extra dollar exchange thus made available is used for purchases of certain Canadian products. We might specify apples, salmon, cheese, fish and certain agricultural products. Then, when payments were resumed, the United Kingdom would be allowed to repay the loans, if she wished, in commodities from her own sterling area, commodities of her own choice provided of course that we can use them. Canada can use most of the goods that she could supply to us.
In conclusion, I want to say that what I have said, Mr. Chairman, is the result of some study and some thought. All that I have said may not be entirely in line with the thinking of the government. Indeed, it may be subject to some correction by the minister when he speaks. But I can assure him that we are interested in this very vital project of expanding our trade as we expand the development of our resources, and maintaining our great agricultural and other industries in this country. With the possibility of international tension easing-let us hope it is a real easing of that tension and let us hope, too, that there will be a diminution of demands for raw materials than can be used
4260	HOUSE OF
Supply-Trade and Commerce for warlike purposes and an increasing demand for materials that can be used in raising the standards of living and the food of that half of the human race which goes to bed hungry every night-it becomes imperative that we should make an annual review of Canada's position as a world trader.
As I have already said, we are third in absolute terms, and first in per capita trade. It is a remarkable achievement for a young country such as this. No government can take credit for it. It has been done because ours is a land which has vast resources, a land peopled by men and women who have done their level best to produce from those resources. I think we can say that it is to the credit of Canadians generally, rather than to the credit of any particular group of Canadians or any particular government in power now or in past days, that we have achieved this remarkable place in the world of commerce. I hope, Mr. Chairman, that we shall continue not only to maintain it but as the days go by to improve our position and make a further contribution to the health and welfare of mankind.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it has been a real pleasure to listen to the two hon. members who thus far have spoken. I may say that it was a real pleasure also to listen to the minister the other night. In the subject of trade, as all hon. members recognize, we are discussing a matter which could easily mean success or disaster to our nation. Perhaps too few people in the country actually comprehend how serious some of the moves we may make in respect of trade can be for all time.
In saying what I shall say here tonight, I have the deepest sympathy for the minister because I realize that he is handling a very difficult task. I believe he is making a good job of it. I realize also that he is not entirely a free agent in drafting policies or in putting them into operation, but is more or less the victim of the will, shall I say, of people who do not understand the problem nearly as well as the minister does.
Now, that being said, I shall go on with what I feel it would be fitting for me to say tonight. With respect to the hon. member for Eglinton, I should say that one of his difficulties was that he said what pretty nearly everyone wishes-yes, of course we want that, but nobody knows how to get it. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar did condescend to begin to tell us something about how it might be done. If in the course of my remarks I give more attention to how it ought to be done, I trust I will not be misunderstood. After all the incessant talk in this house about things that ought to be done, which everyone 14 years
[Mr. Coldwell.l

of age and up knows ought to be done, so often no one has said a word about how to do it. That is about one of the most contemptible things of which you could conceive in a country of this kind and in a house of this kind.
There ought to be some sort of penalty imposed on the members of the house who get up and clamour for something to be done, but never give any idea as to how to do it. They rail about something that is not being done, without giving any idea as to how it could be done. We would shorten the length of these sessions by two-thirds if there were some penalty imposed by the whole house or individual members upon those who would put on such a performance. I grow weary of hearing people cry out for things that everybody knows ought to be done, but who never give an idea how to do them.
I thought it would be quite proper to read a little statement which I believe comes from the Ottawa Journal concerning the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It is rather well put, and no one will mind if I put it on the record. It reads as follows:
Mr. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce, spoke to the national foreign trade convention in New York this week, had this to say about the forthcoming commonwealth conference:
"What Canada wants to see emerge from these commonwealth talks is not a sterling area plan, but something very much bigger, in which North America and the free world generally can play a full part to the advantage of all concerned. This kind of an approach, we firmly believe, has the best chance of success. And that is what I hope will emerge."
I think everybody says "amen". The article goes on:
What is this "something" that is "very much bigger", and just how, specifically, is it to be gained? Mr. Howe doesn't offer a clue. Doesn't as much as hint what Canada will propose.
Strange, too, that Mr. Howe himself is not going to the commonwealth conference, but passing it up for a trade mission to South America early in the new year.
That is no reflection on the minister; that is just the beginning of a discussion of his troubles.
There is another quotation which it might be well to have on the record and to keep in mind in our discussion of our very difficult trade situation. This quotation is called "Foreign aid given by U.S.A.," and reads as follows:
From June 30, 1945, to June 30, 1952 the United States extended grants or credits to a total of $38 billion in foreign aid. That was 11-3 per cent of the $308 billion federal revenue in the seven years and 10-6 per cent of the national expenditures- $329 billion-in that period.
Close to a third of the total aid extended was in the form of loans of which $3 billion has been repaid, making the net amount up to June 30 of this year of $35 billion. Congress has authorized foreign aid in the current fiscal year ending next June 30 totalling $5,800 million, which would raise

the grand total to $40,800 million. Western Europe got the lion's share of the net aid, $25,795 million in grants and credits. Great Britain got a net total of $6,363 million. France was second, Germany third, Japan fourth, Italy fifth.
About $1,091 million went, in the early post-war period, to Russia and other countries no longer friendly. That was 3-1 per cent of the total net foreign aid.
That quotation also was taken from the Alberta Wheat Pool Budget, October 31, 1952. I should like to ask all hon. members to ponder this simple question with me for a few minutes: How long do you think the United States can stand that sort of thing? How long do you think it ought to stand it?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend will not mind my saying that over the same period Canada gave more aid to the world on a population or national income basis than the United States. We are still standing it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
Well, I am not so sure that we are "still standing it". I must say that the pressure which is on the ordinary Canadian today as a result of standing that is simply unbearable. Anyone who does not believe that should just get down among the ordinary people and see what a time they are having paying their rent, buying their coal and paying their taxes. I will tell you, if you get down and find out, get the facts, you will not feel that we can afford to stand that very much longer. As an example, stop to think of the almost unbearable pressure that is placed on a young couple when they have a third child, or a second child; what the cost is to have that child delivered to them, what the cost is to raise it in any sort of way, as a result of the taxation which we are placing on everybody in order to stand this thing. And when you reflect on the effect that is going to have on the population of this nation in the course of 25 or 30 years in terms of Canadians who will grow up to carry the responsibilities which must be borne 25 years from now; when you reflect along those lines, you are not so positively sure that we are "standing it" in a way that we can permanently sustain.
All honour to Canada that we are doing it, but I say to the minister it is just high time the pressure began to be relieved. There must be a way of relieving that pressure. I have said this time and time again, and I will say it to the minister once more in all seriousness: You must not keep the idea that the only place you can get money is in the people's pockets. You must not do it. The United States must not do it. If you do you will wreck the world as surely as we are sitting here tonight. It is no longer a laughing matter, a sneering matter or a matter to 68108-270
Supply-Trade and Commerce be treated lightly; it is a matter that must be met and dealt with positively.
I give these facts merely to show how much is being done, and yet what is being done is not nearly enough. Everybody recognizes that. I have another important quotation that I should like to give just to show the difficulties the minister faces. This one again is from the Alberta wheat pool budget of April 3, 1953 this time, and reads as follows:
About 24 per cent of the Canadian population is dependent for a livelihood to a great degree on exports of Canadian products. This country is more dependent upon the continuation of a large export trade to maintain the standard of living here than are any other peoples in the world.
The above statement was made by G. S. Duncan, chairman of the board of directors of the Massey-Harris Company, in an address to the annual meeting of the Ontario hog producers' association. Mr. Duncan said that his company does 75 per cent of its business with foreign countries. He said 54 per cent of Canadian exports go to the United States and that there is a danger of relying too much on one customer.
It is enough worry to the minister to try to find a market for our wheat, oats, barley, hogs, cheese, and other primary products, but when he also has to go out and try to find markets for our manufactured products, well he is facing a task which is impossible under prevailing circumstances. I believe everybody realizes this.
Having said this much, I wish to tell the minister that I want a great deal more information than he has given in his speech. As a member of the house I think I am entitled to it. I am not able to find any document up to the present time in which I can obtain the information I want. I am going to quote some passages from the minister's speech and ask him some questions concerning these which I would like him to answer, before we finish discussing his department. He must know where to get these answers. At page 4065 of Hansard of April 17, in the second column, he used these words:
This strength has been created in large part by sound policies, and it has buoyed us up during a period when many other countries have suffered setbacks.
I want to know in some detail what these "sound policies" are. You know the statement sounds very beautiful on the radio and looks good in the press. So many statements are so beautiful on the surface that they convey much which the people cannot quite comprehend. We all want to know the details. Then I quote another passage on the same page:
During these years the government has done everything possible to encourage and assist the recovery of our exports to those countries overseas which are our traditional customers.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
I would like to know what the "everything possible" is. Everything possible is a very large order. I want to know whether the minister and the government offered to take British pounds in return for Canadian goods that they want to sell to Britain. That was a suggestion of the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar. That suggestion is thoroughly feasible. It has been offered several times by the hon. member for Acadia and various others. Never a word has been said by the government in answer to that, as far as I know; yet it is a thing which is obviously feasible.
I wonder whether the minister would tell us if he has done that; whether he has offered that. I should like to ask him whether or not Canada has yet offered to Great Britain a proposition similar to the one she gave to Great Britain in world war I. Great Britain wanted $50 million worth of wheat. Canada created the money, bought the wheat from Canadians and gave the wheat to Britain on such terms that Britain could repay in any kind of goods that Canada could receive as soon as Britain could repay. Britain had repaid the debt by 1927.
I have suggested such a proposition several times on the floor of the house. Not one person on the government benches has spent a moment trying to show that that proposal is not completely feasible, because they cannot show it. Why do they not use that device? Have they offered to do that for Great Britain? If they have not done that, they have not done everything possible; and to make that statement is simply to deceive men. And there are many other things that could be done, some things that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned. The minister will have to take a little time to answer all this. He realizes, I think, that members of the House of Commons are ^entitled to a detailed explanation of that statement; and the people are also entitled to it.
Now I should like to read another passage from his speech where, at page 4066, he said:
Canada participated fully in the recent commonwealth economic conference, as hon. members are aware.
I think that is a good place to stop. The minister says that Canada "participated fully". What is the minister talking about when he refers to full participation? What is his meaning? We would like to have that explained. Up to the present time the members of the cabinet have been as silent concerning the matter as mice. What went on at that economic conference? We do not know what Canadians proposed; we do not know what they rejected. We do not know
{Mr. Blackmore.l

what Great Britain proposed. We do not know a thing about this matter, which is so vital in our lives at the present time. I say that every hon. member in this House of Commons and every person in the country is entitled to be told in full the answers I have asked for.
If for example Great Britain asked us to use the imperial preference and we refused to do it, everybody in Canada has a right to know that we refused and why we refused. And if the reason we refused was that there was pressure put upon us by the United States, then everybody has a right to know that, 100 per cent. We should know how that pressure was proposed to be put on, and why.
All this information is necessary in order that we may begin to have wisdom concerning our status in international trade today, and concerning the well-being of the British commonwealth, in whose welfare this nation is so intimately bound up-not with the wellbeing of the United States. We have evidence to show that the United States is pretty hard-boiled, to use a common expression, in her business arrangements. She is not one bit concerned about our well-being. She is concerned about herself, and that is enough. If the United States takes care of herself, she is doing all the worrying she can afford to do. Let us look around and find someone with whom we can work.
Now, I want to know all about this commonwealth economic conference. Why has there been all the secrecy about it? We find secrecy everywhere. That does not sound very good; it does not look good.
I should like to read again from the minister's speech:
We may be greatly encouraged also by the increasing amount of international agreement about what needs to be done to solve the trade and financial problems of the sterling area and western Europe.
Well, what is this thing that "needs to be done?" Who are the nations that are in agreement? To what exent are they in agreement? How do we know they are in agreement? Has their agreement been expressed? If so, how and when? Until the minister gives' detailed information setting forth the answers to those questions he is just deceiving us, leaving us in the dark; and maybe he is deceiving himself, too.
I should like to know what he believes should "be done" to solve the difficult financial problem, the problem of the sterling area and western Europe. I want to know why he thinks that "what" is a solution, and I should like to have evidence to prove that it will be a solution. I think it would do the minister's department a lot of

good if they were to do a bit of hard thinking along that line. I shall be listening; I will not take everything lying down, either. We have to have something that will help us toward the solution of these problems. And now we come to this passage:
Many of the countries concerned are showing signs of moving in the right direction.
What is "the right direction?" Who knows it is the right direction? How does he know? Where did he find out? Where is his proof? Does the fact that half a dozen graduates of the London school of economics in the minister's department think it is the "right direction", make it so? He has half a dozen pretty noisy boys in his department, who think they know all about how to run the world. But they do not know very much yet; they only think they know. I have been in touch with several of them. Of course he has some men in his department who do know, but their voices cannot be heard because of the babble of loud noise from those youngsters who got all their knowledge at the London school of economics, the very last place they ought to go to get the truth. So we .want these facts.
Now on the same page the minister said:
Nevertheless, in 1952 the value, quantity and proportion of our exports to British countries did increase and for the first time their value amounted to over $1 billion.
What I want to know is this. What kind of exports did they accept in large amounts? Were they exports which are the result of our war condition, or exports which are to be permanent? If they are not permanent, then obviously the very minute things begin to clear up in Korea those markets will disappear like mist on a July morning. So if we are not going to be relying upon quicksand as the basis for the house we are going to build, we must be given many of the details.
Another passage at page 4066 is in these words:
I am glad to see that the United Kingdom have been able to increase their sales to us of many types of machinery and that their sales to the United States are increasing. It has been said before, but it bears repeating, that there is a large and continuing market in this country for many goods which the United Kingdom can supply in greater quantities.
I should like to have details about that. I cannot be convinced by this smooth statement. I cannot understand, for example, if it is really true that the British are increasing their sales to us, why it is that we find conditions such as those disclosed in the 68108-2704
Supply-Trade and Commerce February 1953 issue of the Economic Record from Great Britain. It says in respect of sugar:
Sugar is still rationed to 10 ounces each week for each ration book. It is estimated that to deration sugar an additional half million tons a year would be required which can only be obtained from the dollar area at a cost of about $40 million a year.
Why are they not able to get all the sugar they need over there, when we are literally swamped by Cuban sugar here?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext: They have derationed sugar now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE
speechtext:
I am speaking about February of 1953. I am wondering now whether the derationing is on a basis that can persist, or whether they have established conditions under which they can continue to deration. Then in connection with cheese it says:
The weekly ration is now II ounces, with a special allowance of 12 ounces for agricultural and certain other workers in places where there are no catering facilities. The abnormally low level of the ration is due to Britain's inability to spend dollars on cheese from Canada and the United States.
And so on and so on. We go through a list which would make a person feel unhappy for a week. And now Great Britain is "increasing her sales" to us. That needs to be explained in much detail, much more than the minister has given thus far. I read this on page 4066:
Germany has increased its Canadian purchases substantially so that it is now the second largest European market for our products.
I want to know what Germany has paid us for what she has bought from us. What have we taken from Germany that we could not take from Britain? Can we continue to take these things from Germany without interfering with the welfare of any of our own industries? These are things that we all want to know. I quote again from page 4066:
From the Canadian point of view the increasing importance of the Japanese market has become more and more apparent in each recent year.
What are we prepared to accept from Japan that will enable us to sell to Japan? Everyone realizes that it will be a fine thing to trade with a nation of 83 million people, or thereabouts, if we can take the things that they have to send us. We are sure they can take our products, but what goods are they able to send us that Britain or some other nation of the commonwealth is unable to send? Before that statement can be worth very much to me I have to have that question answered. Here is another passage from page 4066:
At every appropriate opportunity the government has made clear to the government of the United

Supply-Trade and Commerce States that basic principles are being infringed by the imposition of import controls upon dairy products in the United States.
I would like to know what "basic principles" are being infringed by the United States when she takes measures to shut out dairy products from Canada. I would like to know what moral responsibility the United States has to Canada that she must allow Canadian dairy products to come in to destroy her dairy producers. I should like the minister to explain that in great detail when he comes to speak. We do not want generalities; we want details, as the minister would want them. The minister is one of the greatest engineers in Canada. He would not accept a blueprint that was blurred or vague in its details. He would want every detail quite clear so he could be sure it would work out in a certain way. The minister is giving us a blueprint for a trading establishment which we want to erect for the welfare of our children and our children's children. We want the details of that blueprint, not just a general statement.
Before leaving this matter may I ask this. Has not the United States merely invoked article XIX in the famous GATT which was designed to enable a nation to protect any of its industries against outside goods? The minister must have read something different from what is contained in the agreement. I think I could get a copy without much difficulty and show that it was definitely declared that any nation had the right to protect any of its industries which were in danger of being destroyed from outside. If there is no such provision, then I suggest that when GATT comes up again we put that provision in and be sure that it stays there. Without that the agreement is not much good. If the United States agreed to GATT, she did it in a moment of absentmindedness and is now finding out that it will not work. She is taking realistic measures to protect her own producers.
This is the system which she used to build herself from a group of straggling colonies into the mightest nation on the face of the earth in an amazingly short time. Are we to be told that those principles which she used to build herself to greatness are no longer sound and that she should now begin to go backwards and undo the things she has done so painfully through the generations, and if she does not do it she is "infringing principles?" All these matters need considerable elaboration. Another passage from page 4067 reads:
Canada and the United States have helped themselves and the world as a whole through the

negotiation of extensive trade agreements, before the war in 1935 and 1938, and since the war under GATT at Geneva in 1947 and at Torquay in 1951. The unprecedented flow of trade between Canada and the United States today is conducted in accordance with the general agreement on tariffs and trade.
That is getting near the climax. I tell you that we need a lot of explaining there. Just how has Canada helped herself through GATT? Let us have the details, even if it does take a book or another white paper. We do not want just a general statement, let us have it proved that Canada has "helped herself" through GATT. At whose expense has Canada helped herself? That is also an important matter. Has it been at the expense of Britain or some other member of the commonwealth? Just how has the United States helped herself through GATT, and at whose expense? Let us have the details.
Does the minister know who originated the idea that led to the instrument called GATT? I wonder if the minister has gone back into history to find out who it was that started this thing called GATT. That is a very important thing to know. If you could find out just who it was in the United States administration that proposed GATT or the thing that grew into GATT, and find out what connection he has, it might make a lot of difference in our thinking in respect to GATT.
Does the minister know what were the immediate objectives of the first movers in this connection? For example, was it the destruction of imperial preferences and the pound sterling? What were the ultimate objectives? For example, were they to give the United States markets? Was it considered that the rest of us did not amount to anything so long as the United States got markets? I wonder if that is true. Can the minister prove that it is not true, with documents that can stand up against criticism?
I suggest that the minister will have some help from these graduates of the London school of economics, but he should be sure to give us both sides. I have not very much faith in the London school of economics.
